subtopic: DELEGATION TO CONSIDER BASIS FOR FEDERAL UNION WITH CANADA

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DELEGATION TO CONSIDER BASIS FOR FEDERAL UNION WITH CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon.
members are aware, the people of Newfoundland some months ago elected a national convention for the purpose of making recommendations to the government of the United Kingdom as to possible forms of the future government of Newfoundland. Subsequently the question of the form of government to be adopted is to be placed before the people of Newfoundland in a referendum.
As announced in this house on April 2 last by my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), the government of Canada has agreed to receive a delegation from the Newfoundland convention to consider and discuss whether there is, in the opinion of all concerned, a fair and equitable basis for federal union of Newfoundland with Canada. Arrangements have now been made to begin discussions on Wednesday, June 25. The delegation will arrive in Ottawa tomorrow. We are happy to have the opportunity of welcoming the delegation on that day since June 24 is being observed this year as the 450th anniversary of the discovery of the island.
It will be recalled that, following the disastrous economic collapse in 1920-30, Newfoundland encountered serious financial difficulties. In 1933, with the approval of the government and legislature of Newfoundland, a royal commission was appointed by the United Kingdom government to inquire into the situation. The commission recommended that responsible government should be suspended and legislative and executive authority be vested in an appointed commission, responsible to the United Kingdom government, until

such time as the island should again become self-supporting. It was also recommended that meanwhile the United Kingdom should assume financial responsibility for the government of the islandi. These recommendations were approved by the Newfoundland legislature and by the United Kingdom parliament. The Newfoundland constitution was accordingly suspended and a commission of government was appointed by the United Kingdom government and assumed office in 1934.
Shortly after the commission was established, most of the Newfoundland debt, which in 1934 stood at about a $100 million, with relatively high interest rates, was converted to a sterling issue at three per cent guaranteed by the United Kingdom as to principal and interest. The United Kingdom also advanced considerable sums for developmental purposes, and up to 1939 met budget deficits totalling over $16 million.
Beginning in 1941, Newfoundland experienced a remarkable recovery. This was due in part to the heavy defence expenditures in Newfoundland and Labrador by Canada and the United States, and in part to the rise in prices of Newfoundland's principal exports, fish and newsprint. Since 1941, Newfoundland has had an annual surplus now amounting to about $29 million. In addition, Newfoundland's debt has been reduced to about $74 million; the public services have been expanded and improved. Revenues which in 1939 were just over $12 million reached $37 million in 1946.
In December 1945 the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs of the United Kingdom announced that in order "to enable the people of Newfoundland to come to a free and informed decision. . . on their future form of government" a national convention would be elected in Newfoundland in the spring of 1946. The terms of reference of the convention are as follows:
To consider and discuss amongst themselves, as elected representatives of the Newfoundland people, the changes that have taken place in the financial and economic situation of the island since 1934, and, bearing in mind the extent to which the high revenues of recent years have been due to wartime conditions, to examine the position of the country and to make recommendations to His Majesty's government as to possible forms of future government to be put before the people at a national referendum.
It will be seen from the terms of reference that the convention does not itself have authority to decide Newfoundland's future form of government. The convention is empowered merely to make recommendations to the United Kingdom government as to possible forms of future government. It is

Newfoundland
conceivable that the convention may recommend one form, or alternative forms. In any event, whatever form or forms of government are recommended', the decision as to its acceptance is to be left to the people of Newfoundland themselves.
The convention, except for short periods of adjournment, has now been meeting continuously since September last. With a view to reaching an informed opinion on Newfoundland's economic and financial position, the convention has completed exhaustive inquiries into various phases of Newfoundland's economy, and its progress under the commission of government. The convention has come now to the second stage of its inquiry, namely a consideration of Newfoundland's constitutional future. In May of the present year a delegation from the convention visited the United Kingdom to seek information concerning the financial and fiscal arrangements which might be expected to exist between the United Kingdom and Newfoundland' under alternative forms of future government. That delegation has reported1 to the convention.
The delegation which will arrive in Ottawa tomorrow will consist of Hon. F. G. Bradley, K.C., who led the delegation to London, and six other members of the convention. The six other members of the delegation to Ottawa were not members of the London delegation. They are Mr. J. R. Smallwood, secretary of the delegation; Mr. T. G. W. Ashbourne, Mr. C. H. Ballam, Rev. L. Burry, Mr. P. W. Crummey, and Mr. G. F. Higgins, K.C.
I have asked the following members of the government to act as a committee to meet with the delegation from Newfoundland: the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister of Fisheries and the leader of the government in the Senate.
An atmosphere of mutual friendliness and understanding will, I am sure, characterize the forthcoming discussions. The peoples of Canada and of Newfoundland are closely associated through strong and enduring ties. We owe a common allegiance to the crown and have a common heritage of British political and legal institutions. We have many close personal, professional and commercial associations. We are neighbours in a North American environment. We face many common problems. We have memories of dangers shared and victories won together. These associations afford a broad basis for full and
frank discussion of many of the considerations of which, in the event of union, account would have to be taken by both countries.
The Newfoundland delegates, having, with their colleagues in the convention, studied intensively the problems and prospects of Newfoundland, will be able to throw much light on the questions to be explored. They will have an opportunity to learn at first hand about the working of the Canadian federal system and will thus be in a better position to advise their colleagues on what would be involved for their country in the event of union. As a result of the discussions the Canadian people also will be in a better position to appreciate what would be involved for Canada were Newfoundland to become a province. The Newfoundland delegation will report their views of the situation to the national convention. It will remain for the convention to recommend to the government of the United Kingdom whether the question of union with Canada should be referred to the people of Newfoundland for a decision.
The question of Newfoundland's future form of government is of course one for the people of Newfoundland themselves to decide. It is not a matter in which either the people of Canada or the government of Canada would wish to interfere. Should the question become a matter of referendum, whatever the decision might be, it would be received by the government and people of Canada with understanding and good will.
On the part of Canada no final decision would of course be taken without the approval of parliament. Section 146 of the British North America Act makes provision for procedure in the event of the admission of Newfoundland to the union. So far as Canada is concerned, the action provided for in this section is an address by both houses of parliament.

speechtext:
Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 337, to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932, and the Foreign Insurance Companies Act, 1932.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a short and simple bill to enable Canadian insurance companies and other insurance companies operating in Canada to invest their funds in securities of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development. The immediate purpose in asking parliament to approve this legislation is to enable our Canadian companies doing business in the United States to use their funds in that country to buy securities which the bank is to issue shortly in the United States for the first time. The other objective is, of course, to facilitate the long run purposes for which the international bank was established, that is, the reconstruction and development of member countries and the promotion and growth of international trade. We expect that Canada will benefit both directly in our export trade and indirectly in other respects from the accomplishment of these purposes.
I should recall to hon. members that Canadian insurance companies under section 60 of our act are permitted to invest their funds in a fairly wide variety of high grade securities. These include, first, bonds and other securities issued or guaranteed by governments -Canadian, British and foreign-including provincial and state governments. Secondly, they include bonds secured by mortgages and various types of statutory payments. Thirdly, they include debentures, preferred and common stock of corporations with certain specified dividend records, and subject to certain limitations. Finally, of course, there are 83166-287
included mortgages and hypothecs on real estate, not exceeding sixty per cent of the value of the property. A company may not invest in bonds or other obligations on which payment of interest or capital is in default. There are various detailed provisions relating to these items and one or two other minor items specified in the law, but what I have said will serve as a brief outline of the nature of the eligible securities.
When these categories of securities were drawn up there was, of course, no international corporation of the nature of the International Bank in existence, and since our list was specified in fairly detailed terms there was no class which includes the securities to be issued by the bank. While the securities issued or guaranteed by the bank resemble in certain respects foreign government bonds which our insurance companies are permitted to hold, they do not come within the present provisions of our law, and this bill is intended to bring them within it.
I should point out that in the United States, where jurisdiction on these matters rests with the state governments, action has been taken already by a number of the more important state legislatures to make the securities o.f the international bank eligible investments for insurance companies. I understand that this has been done by the states of New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and California, among others, while the legislation of several other states, including Connecticut and Delaware, already permits investment [DOT] in the bank's securities without specific amendment.
I do not think it is necessary for me to describe the nature, functions or activities of the international bank at this time. The house is already familiar with its purpose and constitution, which were, of course, approved when parliament authorized our participation in it by the Bretton Woods Agreements Act of 194o. I tabled a few weeks ago a report to parliament on operations under that act during the last fiscal year. There is a large amount of published information available on the bank, its financial condition, the loan it has already made to France, and its other activities.
I should make it quite clear that the bill now being proposed simply enables insurance companies to buy securities of the international bank if in their judgment the securities are a good investment on the terms at which they are offered. My own view is that the securities to be issued by the bank should command a high rating. Behind them will stand, first of all, the assets of the bank, inttOLLiaa Q3SIA3H
Insurance Companies Act

eluding not only those loans made and other assets acquired with the funds borrowed by the bank through the sale of securities, but also the loans and other assets representing the paid-in capital	of	the	bank	and	itsreserves. I have no doubt that the management and directors	of	the	bank	will	do
everything that is humanly possible to ensure that loans are wisely made and wisely spent. But those who devised the bank's constitution some three years ago recognized that more than normal risks and uncertainties would be involved in the granting of international loans during the post-war reconstruction period, and special care was taken to provide safety for those who invested in the bank's securities.
For example, the bank is able to call upon those governments which are members of it to pay amounts up to four times the total of the capital they have already paid in, if this is required to meet the obligations of the bank. The constitution of the bank limits its loans or guarantees to a total not exceeding its unimpaired subscribed capital, plus its reserves and surplus, and this in effect sets a limit on the bank's obligations to investors. Moreover, even within this limit, the security market itself, in determining the total amount of the bank's securities which it will accept over the course of time, will thereby determine the degree to which investors in those securities will be protected by the obligations of the United States, Canadian and other governments to put up additional capital if that should be required.
I should also point out that this legislation does not in any way override the control of capital movements or foreign investment by Canadians under the Foreign Exchange Control Act. Insurance companies having funds in the United States will, when this bill is passed, be able to invest such funds in the securities of the bank. However, if a company wished to transfer funds from Canada to purchase the bank's securities, it would need to . secure permission from the foreign exchange control board, and under present circumstances sales of United States funds for capital transactions of this kind could not be permitted.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF 1932 STATUTES TO AUTHORIZE INVESTMENT IN SECURITIES OF RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT BANK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be but a short time this afternoon, but I do want to call the attention of the house to the great danger of this bill. It will affect the life insurance companies of this country and every policyholder in those companies. We have been through some very trying times since 1932. This is not the time to bring a measure like this before the house.

It should go to the committee on banking and commerce for consideration, because it affects the whole consolidated debt of this country and every insurance company's future. We are dealing now with trust funds. No one knows yet whether or not this international bank is going to be a success. It is becoming doubtful about the united nations as we see its futility. We had the Dumbarton Oaks and the Bretton Woods agreements which were agreed to by this house in December, 1945, and the creation of an international bank.
I have a number of objections to this proposal. When the minister introduced the resolution I pointed out that these were trust funds. I asked whether the superintendent of insurance had sanctioned the measure, and he said yes. I want to point out to the house the very grave danger which affects every policyholder if this particular bill goes through. We should stop and listen before it is too late.
These companies do business outside of as well as within Canada. The bill proposes to permit insurance companies to invest in bonds, debentures and other securities issued by the international bank. When I spoke on the Bretton Woods agreements on December 6, 1945, I said:
I am not opposed to an international monetary mechanism being established to solve the economic conditions which are growing out of the war, but I am opposed to the present proposals and I propose to show the reasons why and give the view of two great British chancellors of the exchequer.
Then I went on to refer to the agreement which was made, and I said it would mean the end of British preference and would place Canada in a very dangerous position. This bill refers to two statutes. During the session of 1932 there was a consolidation of the two statutes which are affected by this bill, and those statutes will be found in the statutes for 1932. The principle of this bill is set out in sections 1, 2 and 3; it amends the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932 and the Foreign Insurance Companies Act, 1932. There are two schedules to the act of 1932, one dealing with assets and the other with reserves. The Bretton Woods Agreements Act in chapter 11 of the statutes of 1945.
The minister has said that the inspector of insurance has approved this bill. I was very much surprised to hear that, because these are trust funds. The policyholders should have something to say about this. There should be a meeting of shareholders in order that they might approve this proposal. I am not opposed to the settlement of debt by international monetary machinery to remedy the economic

Insurance Companies Act
conditions growing out of the war, but I oppose this way of doing it. There will be no more preferential trade.
I was not a member of the house in 1932 when all the trouble arose over losses of insurance companies abroad. All these life companies must report to the inspector every year and obtain a certificate in order to do business. I have the report here but I will not name the companies; I will refer to them only as companies A, B, C and D. Hon. members can get a copy of the report of the superintendent of insurance and see how money was being lost in 1932. Practically every bank has a trust company connected with or related to it, and after the Home Bank failure great losses were shown by banks and insurance companies through common stock investments of this type.
During the depression of 1923 we had the failure of the Home bank when thousands of shareholders lost millions of dollars. Depositors suffered and millions of dollars were lost by frauds abroad. I introduced a bill in this House of Commons regarding lapsed insurance policies, the details of which will be found in Hansard, of February 14, 1929, page 123. I also introduced later a bill to prohibit investments by insurance companies and banks in common stocks outside Canada. The Liberal party was in opposition then. One of the speakers in the debate was Mr. Hepburn-page 1102, March 14, 1932- who was then a private member of the house; he criticized severely some of the investments of the insurance companies. Other members who spoke were Mr. Bennett, Mr. Ralston, Mr. Spencer and Mr. Lawson. I am not going to refer to what was said then, because that is past history. But it warns us of the great and grave danger of allowing banks and trust and insurance companies to go on without any restrictions in the manner indicated.
I do not believe in the principle of this bill. The government brought in the Bretton Woods bill in December 1945. The United States had then about ninety-five per cent of the gold supply of the world at Fort Knox. I gave my reasons for opposing the Bretton Woods agreement at that time, and was supported by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) in a note on December 8, 1945. This bill will cause the gravest concern to every policyholder in a life insurance company in Canada. Millions of dollars are already invested by Canadian life insurance companies in the United States and other countries. The companies are named at the following pages of the inspector's report: 93, 110, 134, 178, 181, 185, 193 and 255. Also the investments outside Canada are given, 83166-287J
total liabilities outside Canada, ledger assets, non-ledger investments, and so forth running into hundreds of millions of dollars. All these assets are affected by this bill. The inspector's report speaks for itself.
There was to be a conference at Moscow on international debts. It failed completely, and has been postponed to meet in London in November. Russia and France and the United States, according to the Ottawa Journal, are going to meet in Paris on June 24 to discuss European debt, settlement on the Marshall plan, and so forth. What I do not like about this bill is that it brings up once again the old question of the debts incurred by Britain in the first world war, and the matter of lend-lease; and involved in that question is the further question of bases from Newfoundland to British Guiana. Apparently that question has been written into the debt and no doubt the international bank will be asked to come across with sufficient money to take care of the settlement of that whole question'-involving both wars and lend-lease accounts. I am afraid it is going to cause a great deal of trouble. The bill is based also on the principles of the successor to the old league of nations, and the success of the bill hinges upon the success of the UNO. That will be seen by reference to many of the sections of the bill. After the last war we had the league of nations and following this war we have a new league proposal entirely, in the UNO. The result of the general policy that is now being proposed will be, in my opinion, the end of preferences and the dissolution of the empire. The result of Bretton Woods will be the abolition of the British preference and preferential trade within the empire.
We are told that the United States is in full accord with this bill. Why not? It is the most favourably situated of all the nations today. It is the supreme creditor nation in the world and can therefore dictate its own terms. When the minister introduced the bill the other day I pointed out what in my opinion were certain errors that had to be guarded against. It is all very well to say that the forty-eight states of the American union agree to it, but we should not forget that their banks and insurance companies have not the stability that our financial institutions have always had. Far from it.
In my opinion this is the wrong time to bring forward this bill. In 1932 there was a great deal of criticism of the investments of insurance companies in common stocks not only within Canada but outside as well. The situation was indeed a serious one. To qualify for an annual certificate some companies put down common
Insurance Companies Act

stocks at high rates. An order in council passed in 1932 allowed certain preferences in statements of book, par and market values of stock. One stock I know of went down from 98 to 7 or 8 in the market, yet 98 was quoted by one company to gain a certificate. You can see therefore the liability of the insurance companies for these investments. They are handling trust funds and everyone who has a policy is affected by any error in judgment which these companies may perpetrate in relation to the international bank. I venture to call this whole matter a tragedy in international affairs. I do not think it is too much to say that the policy now proposed will mean the end of the British preference and! preferential trade and the end of the present British empire.
What is this proposal before us today? The united nations monetary and financial conference, held at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, from July 1 to July 22, 1944, resulted in certain articles of agreement. Those articles were approved by the 'United States Senate on July 20, 1945, and by Canada in December 1945. The proposals provide for an international monetary fund or multilateral clearing and for an international bank for reconstruction and development. The fund will provide short-term credits and the bank will provide long-term loans for countries whose balance of payments is adverse. The fund and the bank are the nucleus, or an organ, of an internationalist federation whose chief function is to give unrestricted scope to the gold standard, and expansionist policies of the principal creditor. Participation in the fund by monetary quota is to be the determining and limiting factor.
The articles of agreement involve a return to the gold standard. Monetary and economic policy is to be enforced throughout the world by an international authority supported by an international policy force and by the equivalent of world government. The fund and the bank will be situated in and controlled by the United States as a result of that country's 85 per cent holding of the world's monetary gold. The favourable balances that the United States will enjoy will be sustained by American loans to foreign, countries. Imperial preference and the sterling area will be abandoned. International currency stabilization should be based on: (1) sound financial administration such as is provided within the sterling area; (2) effective trade reciprocity which has been successfully achieved by imperial preference; (3) stability of the price level and a managed gold standard.
I do not think there is very much more I can say except to state emphatically that I

am thoroughly opposed to the bill. This whole Bretton Woods business is the creation of Lord Keynes. He thought he had an idea and they sent him to Washington. They had a number of meetings covering a period of seven weeks at Bretton Woods. Keynes is no doubt a great financier but he has never had any faith in the British empire. A critic said editorially at the time of his death: "The death of Lord Keynes occurred at the end of April. He had been our principal negotiator with the Americans about the loan. For this task he was, in spite of his excellent brain, very much handicapped, for as I have said, he had no faith in the future of the empire, nor indeed any urge to stand by it. And this lack of faith, this pessimism showed all through his life. He did not fight for his country when he was a young man, and when he was older he did not appear to rely on the essential qualities of his countrymen. He could work for them, but he could not believe in their future. This attitude of his did us immense harm in Washington. Many Americans felt that they need not consider the empire when England's principal negotiator disbelieved it. Added to this he was accompanied to Washington by a crowd of superior young men, economists, professors and others who made an indelible, and deplorable, impression upon all who saw them and heard their haughty and highbrow voices. We make a great mistake when we send such representatives abroad. We cannot make ourselves popular in the United States, there is too deep a prejudice there against Britain, but the sort of people she sent to the United States to discuss the loan would be disliked anywhere and were fatal in America. Lord Keynes may not have been aware of this but the attaches of the British embassy, the men who are trained to have quiet good manners and patience, suffered acutely.
This 'bill has come up at a most inopportune time and I suggest it could very well_ have been held over. There was no necessity to proceed with it at this session. I had been hoping that we would get through with this session by the first of July. If the bill were allowed to stand over I do not think it would affect Britain's financial relations with the United States to the slightest degree, because the questions involved in the bill could be ironed out at the meeting now in Paris and the one that is to take place next November in London. An attempt was made to settle international debts in Moscow but that failed. I suggest that for twenty years we have had too many international meetings,

Insurance Companies Act
peace pacts, financial agreements and all that kind of thing. They have all ended in failure.
The question of lend lease is also involved, so that at this particular time it can only lead to trouble if we proceed with this bill, because after all the principles are inconsistent. In my opinion imperial preference and, indeed, the very existence of the empire are now at stake. I do not wish to say very much more about this matter but I am certainly absolutely opposed to the principle of the bill. It can only mean trouble for the mother country. Russia is too weak to fight anyone at the present time, having lost twenty million men in the war. Her cities destroyed by Germany are all rubble; she has no real houses; the people have no homes, and the result will be that the bank will have to make provision for them as well as for rebuilding all of Europe. Russia is too weak to fight anybody at the present time. If she had superior armaments and were to attempt it, she might come to the point of disaster. But it does seem that the Soviet Union is not the enemy of all the rest. She is only the enemy of two different ideologies. I am glad to see the announcement that the day of appeasement by Britain and the United States is over and that they are going to settle with her in the right way by negotiation and all that kind of thing. I hope we shall see Russia, the United States and Britain carry into peace the successes which they had in war. No purpose can be served by criticizing Russia, because if there is any good left in her she cannot afford not to develop it. If not, nothing else matters. Our task as an empire is to work with the United States and France, we hope, not so much for the rehabilitation of Germany-we did that before and saw the result-our task is to work with our allies in the war, and not do as was done after the last war, rebuild Germany at the expense of France. Britain now after 1945 seems bent on making the same mistake as after 1918.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF 1932 STATUTES TO AUTHORIZE INVESTMENT IN SECURITIES OF RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT BANK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is interesting in this sense, that it shows a new trend in banking. International banking in the first place had been moving from London to New York; now it is going to Washington. The international bank means that the United States, with the assistance of a few of the other united nations, will finance the devastated countries of Europe and other continents. I remember that before the first war most of the investments of the English insurance companies were in Canada, where they
promoted Canadian trade and Canadian business at large. But since the last war the trend of British investments has been different. Now the money which is paid on premiums by the Canadian people is often diverted, according to the decisions made by the insurance companies, to countries other than Canada, countries rvith which Canada has little trade.
Statistics are dry, but when we compile them in order to understand the various trends of business we inevitably come to certain conclusions. In my humble view the money which is paid by Canadians on premiums should be used to promote the interests of the Canadian people at large, either in this country or in other countries with which we are associated in trade and business. Some time ago it was the practice that all earnings of insurance companies in Canada were deposited in Canadian chartered banks whose main offices are in the various cities of Canada. Now it is different. A subagent of a mother bank in London is used for the investments of the insurance companies. In the monthly reports which are published in the Montreal Gazette it is most interesting to note that the total amount of the current and savings deposits of that subagency of an English mother bank is the lowest of all the banks, probably because of the fact that some time in the month the money which is deposited in that bank is sent across to the mother house in England.
What I regret about that institution, which is known to everybody, is that it does not give the same reports as the other Canadian banks give. Its report is mimeographed, and it is a summary; it is far from being complete. The purposes of the establishment of that new institution-which I will not call a bank, because it is rather a subagency of a big London bank-is to drain off to London all the Canadian investments kept with that bank, and in London the money is reinvested according to the decision not of Canadian bankers but of English bankers. I protest against that.
I warn the minister of the danger of such investments which cannot be in accordance with Canadian needs. I say that for this reason. I do not know what will be the purpose of the English companies making any investments in the international bank. There again we may have a representative, but we shall not be the majority in that bank and we may wonder if the investments which will be made by the international bank will be in conformity with Canadian needs.
Insurance Companies Act

I draw the attention of the minister and my hon. colleague to this serious question, because the amount of premiums paid by the Canadian people to insurance companies is high; and there is a surplus of money which belongs to the insurance company and which may be profitable to Canadian business. Very often it is hard for us to get from the insurance companies any loans, for housing, for instance. If the insurance companies are given the excuse of being permitted to make investments in the international bank, when the Canadian people go to the insurance companies to get housing loans they will be told, "It is impossible; we have lent all our money to the international bank for the reconstruction of Europe," or some other continent, and the Canadian people will have to wait longer in order to see the fulfilment of the promises made by the insurance companies.
That is one point. I do not want to repeat what I have said. I believe this is a matter to which members of both houses should give serious attention. They should consider what would be the best possible investment for all insurance companies which operate in this country.
Lately we have seen in the press that the largest investment in Canadian business has been made by United States companies operating in Canada, just as before the war it was by English companies operating in Canada. We should come back to the old practice. The new one is wrong, because we cannot dispose of our assets as well as we could previously. The minister has control over the investments of the insurance companies so long as they are made in Canadian business here in this country; but when they are made outside, when by law we authorize insurance companies to make investments in the international bank, we have no more control. We have a representative there but he counts only for one, and the decision is made by the other nations which at times are very greedy and leave nothing to Canada. The international bank is an institution for which we pay and from which we get nothing except investments in countries with which we may have some trade, but it is doubtful. Therefore, sir, the only way to be practical is to come back to the old theory of true Canadian government and as far as possible have all the investments of the insurance companies made to assist Canadian business men.
My second point, which I suggested some years ago to a predecessor of the minister, is that we should tax Lloyd's, a company that has been operating in Canada but which does not pay taxes. It is not a company; it is a society, and I have been told that is the

reason Lloyd's does not come within the taxation laws. I do not see why a group of men, called a society or a company, should not pay the same taxes that Canadian companies pay. Otherwise their competition becomes unfair. If they do not pay taxation their rates may be lower than those of the Canadian companies or even other English companies that are taxed; and it is disloyal competition for our own firms. I will tell you more than that, sir, as to why no special consideration should be given Lloyd's. Some time ago a Norwegian company was ready to come here and register its ships in Canada, but Lloyd's objected and said, "We will not insure your ships if they are of Canadian register." Therefore I do not see why we should have special consideration for a company such as that, which does all the promotion of English business but forgets everything when it comes to the Canadian side of it.
I bring both these matters to the attention of the minister-the taxation of Lloyd's and the consideration of Canadian interests in connection with investments by insurance companies.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF 1932 STATUTES TO AUTHORIZE INVESTMENT IN SECURITIES OF RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT BANK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I noted with some interest what the minister had to say in reference to the passing of this bill and the promotion of international trade. I am of the opinion that when our citizens make their payments to the insurance companies, which become these trust funds, they believe that such payments are in accordance with the law as it now stands. They will not have the opportunity to review what is in this bill, and perhaps will never know that the legislation before us today will permit those in charge-presumably the government, since this looks like a government bill-to use their trust funds in the promotion and bolstering up of an- international bank. That is not their intention. In my opinion they feel that trade would be expanded much -more if these premiums and trust funds were invested in this country of resources and opportunity, which investment I am sure the minister will agree is recognized by this parliament as one that may be made by insurance companies. In that way we would retain these moneys here, where the trustees feel they belong, rather than having them invested in an international bank.
A few moments ago the hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot) brought up an even more important point, which with the permission of the house I should like to repeat. We have sat in thi3 chamber listening to speech after speech about the shortage of

Insurance Companies Act
houses and the scarcity of cheap money with which to build them. We have heard about what is more or less the flop of Housing Enterprises-a company financed by the insurance companies-because those insurance companies were not getting a sufficient return on their money to permit them to go ahead and build more houses in spite of the obstacles of high labour costs and so on. Yet today we are asked to pass legislation which will let this money go into another channel when it is so badly needed here for housing and other enterprises that are awaiting expansion. They are awaiting expansion not only by our own people but also by those who are so anxious to come here from Great Britain. Today we see in the press that some seven thousand people are coming to Canada from the British isles. They will bring every dollar they can possibly get hold of; but how many dollars will they be permitted to bring with them, in view of the financial condition of England today? Can each individual bring So,000 in Canadian money? I doubt it. They have British pounds to burn over there, but they cannot change them into Canadian dollars in Britain, and we on this side cannot exchange dollars for British pounds for the development of this country. No; they must have wheat and bacon for every Canadian dollar they are able to get their hands on, and they cannot allot Canadian dollars to their people who are so anxious to come to Canada.
I remember the discussion in 1932, when the previous bill was under discussion, when we -were over there and you were over here; and remembering that discussion I wonder that hon. gentlemen opposite have the audacity to introduce the present bill, which goes against every principle enunciated by the great Liberal party when they were on this side of the house. Hour by hour, speaker by speaker, they berated the Sun Life and all the other life insurance companies who were seeking the legislation enacted at that time. Now I ask hon. members opposite to rise in their places and repeat what they said in 1932, as my honourable and honest friend from Tepriscouata rose in his place today and made his representations.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) pointed out today that forty-eight states of the union gave authorization of the kind proposed in this bill. I do not think that is correct, and I believe the minister will agree with me. I do not believe half the states in the union up to this time have put through similar legislation. But if they have, what of it? Some of us have lived long
enough to see what is happening. I am not speaking in a derogatory fashion about any state of the union, but I do point out What has happened in the individual states. We have seen certain states allow companies to form; we have seen permission given for certain transactions along monetary lines. In the course of a decade that same monetary legislation given passed by the individual states has fallen by the wayside. Today Canadian life insurance policies, next to dominion government bonds, are the soundest investments in this country. But people in many states of the union have suffered for lack of legislation which would protect them as Canadian citizens are protected. State legislation on these matters is not at all on a par with legislation which has emanated from this chamber, for the simple reason that banking legislation applies universally across Canada whereas in the United States it may apply to the individual state. And until such time as the forty-eight states of the union endorse legislation of this kind, and if possible have Washington, as a matter of high policy endorse it, I do not see why we in this country should, to use the language of the street, stick our necks out. We should hold in Canada what we have.
Our banking institutions are recognized the world over as of the highest order. They are on a par with or even higher than those of any other country. Our life insurance organizations are considered equal to or even better than some of those in dear old England.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will realize that certain companies are able to form in England and do business in this country. Do they take risks here after inspection by their own officers or upon inspection by accredited agents in this country? No. They will take a risk in Canada because a certain insurance company may accept a risk on a certain property, for, we will say, $100,000. The Canadian tariff company will take the risk at S100,000 because its organization has examined the risk and has found the rate fair. They go to the expense of checking all the hazards. Those expenses come out of t'he coffers of Canadian insurance companies.
My hon. friend mentioned a case-and I verify it-where a company overseas will take, we will say, $50,000 of a certain risk for the simple reason that the Canadian company was prepared to accept that risk. The Canadian company operates at its own expense; and then the United States and British companies, without any expense whatsoever, will proceed to write a risk on the same property.
Insurance Companies Act

What is more, they write the risk today, and in five years time they renew it, without any inspection or notice to those insured.
There have been cases in which warranty clauses have been slipped in, to the effect that if any of the others carrying a portion of the risk find it necessary to reduce that risk by a certain amount, the risk on which the warranty clause appears will be reduced automatically by the same amount. Who reads insurance policies? I believe the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) will agree that they are like something written on ice. No one reads those great long documents. They are not checked carefully. The owner may not be notified of such a warranty clause slipped in by a company in the United States or the United Kingdom. What I am saying may not be strictly relevant to the bill, but the point I make is that before we become too greatly involved in joint arrangements of this kind, which to my mind are not necessary, we should have an overhauling of the entire insurance system. Let us be on a parity with those who wish to join with us in the manner mentioned in the bill, so that we may feel that not only shall we have fair protection, but that the protection we do get, whether in respect of life, fire or indemnity, is of a kind which has been subject to the examination of our authorities. In this way we may be assured that we shall have the highest type of insurance coverage, such as is found in Canadian fire, life or indemnity policies, a coverage better than that found anywhere else in the world.
Let us keep this money in Canada. Let us not make it easy or soft for those conducting insurance operations to sit at their mahogany desks and control funds for which the minister is responsible. Let them be up and doing in their own line of business. Let them invest their trust funds as the people of Canada would want them invested, namely in Canadian enterprise of a kind which would be considered proper and right by the people of this country. Let us have money for the building of houses, first mortgage money, new enterprise money. Let us retain our Canadian money here for development, in view of the fact that at the present time we cannot get enough United States dollars for goods and services we would send to that country. Let there be some uniformity in the insurance legislation of this international body, before we become too greatly involved.

speechtext:
Mr. speaker. I believe the Social Credit group made its stand clear with respect to the Bretton Woods agreement when the bill was before the house. I realize that at this time it

would not be in order to enter into a discussion of the international monetary fund and international banking. It has been said that the international bank would help to extend foreign trade. I believe all hon. members realize that the situation which has resulted from the shortage of United States dollars can never be remedied by an international monetary fund or an international bank of reconstruction. Apparently it is now recognized that we should help Europe by some form of mutual aid or lend-lease agreement.
When we were discussing the Bretton Woods agreement hon. members of this group stated time and again that the devastated countries of Europe could never overcome their difficu-ties through the Bretton Woods agreement. The only way to overcome them is by some form of mutual aid or lend lease. I remember when we pointed that out we were referred to as idealistic; it was said that we would never be able to get the other countries to agree to such proposals. I just want to remind the house that the stand we took three years ago on this question is being fully substantiated today when it is recognized on all sides that the devastated areas of Europe will have to be helped either by outright gilts or by some form of mutual aid. The kind of help they are able to obtain form the international monetary fund or the international bank will be merely a drop in the bucket.
We in this group oppose the bill generally on the ground that it will aggravate further our exchange position with the United States.
I think the minister has stated that these insurance companies already have funds in the United States, but on the other hand I do not think the minister can guarantee that no Canadian funds will be used for the purpose of buying these securities. To the extent that Canadian funds are used for the purchase of securities of the international bank you will have to make those funds convertible into the currency of any other member state of the bank. That will mean generally that Canadian funds will have to be converted into United States funds. We are already facing a deficit of over $600 million with the United States, and if conditions continue we shall have to face one of $900 million by the end of the year. Therefore I cannot see much sense in bringing down a bill which will aggravate that situation. I think the minister appreciates that that is a serious situation; at least he emphasized it in his budget speech.
Then there is the other argument that it ia not wise at this time to encourage the invest-

Insurance Companies Act
ment of Canadian funds in foreign securities. There is a great need for the investment today of Canadian funds in Canada because there are many projects that need developing. Why should' we encourage Canadians to invest their funds out of the country when there are so many projects needing development here? Remember, the minister's predecessor empha-sibed the fact that we would have to get United States capital into this country to provide us with venture capital. If we are continually to encourage people to invest their money in gilt-edged securities such as dominion bonds and securities of the international bank, we shall find it that much harder to get venture capital in this country.
So far as this group is concerned we are very much opposed to encouraging American capital to come into this country, because that merely means going into debt to the United States, thereby increasing our external debt. By encouraging people to invest their money in dominion bonds or the securities of the international bank you are discouraging the investment of Canadian venture capital in this country.
Will the minister indicate whether it is intended to refer this bill to the banking and commerce committee?

speechtext:
This bill, involving millions of dollars, should not have been brought in in the dying days of this session, but having been brought in, it should go to the banking and commerce committee. What have the forty-eight states of the United States of America to do with Canada? This means the disso-83166-288
lution of the British empire. We are Canadians, a part of the British empire. Evidently the government now has no confidence in this international bank, and wants to unload it on the insurance companies as well. The more I think of it the more it reminds me of the man that broke the bank at Monte Carlo. Our insurance companies are dealing with trust funds, and we have no right to go over the heads of the shareholders and policyholders in those companies, with hundreds of millions of dollars of assets involved. According to statements made in the debate of 1932, one of these companies was on the verge of insolvency in that year on account of the way they had conducted their business. Parliament in the dying days of the session of 1945 put through the Bretton Woods agreement. That was not a settlement of international debts and never will be. It simply means that the United States, holding nearly ninety per cent of the world's gold supply, will be creditor to the whole civilized world. We should stop, look and listen before we interfere with our insurance policies, because that is what this is going to do. The government are afraid of the Bretton Woods policy which they supported in 1945 and are loading the responsibility now on to the insurance companies, which are hard enough pressed as it is to remain efficient after going through two world wars. Our first debt is to the policyholders and shareholders of these insurance companies. Again I ask that this bill be sent to the banking and commerce committee.

There is no intention of sending this bill to the banking and commerce committee. As I said in my brief remarks on introducing the bill, it is a very simple one. It is purely enabling legislation to authorize the insurance companies, if they see fit, to invest in the securities of this international bank. This house approved the two institutions set up in the Bretton Woods Agreement Act of 1945, and approved this international bank. Along with the other members we have undertaken to introduce appropriate legislation to authorize our financial institutions, if they see fit to do so, to invest in the'securities of this bank. As I pointed out in my opening remarks, its securities will be to a very large extent government guaranteed securites. The bank is set up on the principle that the members are responsible for four times their capital subscription. The United States subscription was $3,175 million, of which they have paid in

$635 million, and the balance is of course callable if it should be needed. This institution, whatever some members may think of it, is an attempt to restore the world to ordered trading conditions. It is perfectly true, as the hon. member for Acadia pointed out, that it cannot do the whole job, but it can help, and I for one strongly feel that Canada, which has perhaps more to gain by stable world trading conditions than any other country in the world, should do her part to see that this institution is a success. For that reason this legislation is introduced.

speechtext:

country. But there is another phase upon which I should like the minister to express his view, and that is with regard to our own requirements in Canada. The funds of life insurance companies represent the savings of our people. They are surplus funds which if not immediately invested in the country from which they come will necessarily lead to a depression. I think therefore in keeping with the Bretton Woods agreement, and in keeping also with the international bank, the Canadian government should have set up, indeed should now set up, an investment board or investment bank publicly owned which will see to it that all the life insurance funds in Canada continue to be immediately invested to maintain our own economic system at home, and when that has been taken care of there is no reason why anybody should object to our doing our international part in any financial project which may lead toward the stability of trading between nations. But I do say that a very important point is involved, that it is possible that the funds which should be reinvested in Canada may be drained off and our own country left without the necessary purchasing power to keep our economic system going.

As its name implies, this is an international bank for reconstruction and development. It is not to provide loans for the purchase of wheat, for example, or to negotiate a wheat agreement. It is an institution that is new. Nothing of its sort has been tried before, and it is hoped that it will help to provide financial resources for the war-devastated1 countries in Europe to enable them to reconstruct their economies and do what is necessary to produce goods to export to us in order to pay for goods that we may
Insurance Companies Act

send them. The hon. member wishes to know why we should do it now. For this reason. We are a partner, along with many other nations, in this International Bank for Reconstruction and Development. It is about to make its first issue of securities to the public, and if I may express a personal view I think it is desirable that we should take our place along with the other partners and not have it said in the United States that they are the only people who are doing anything in this direction. We must not have them say, "We are going to put up all the money while Canada is not doing anything about it". We are a partner in the thing and we have an interest as great as or greater than that of almost any other country in working out suitable financial relations; and, having approved the principle two years ago, we must I think take our proper part in carrying it into effect. subtopic: AMENDMENT OF 1932 STATUTES TO AUTHORIZE INVESTMENT IN SECURITIES OF RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT BANK
speechtext:
The object of this bill is to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act of 1932 and the Foreign Insurance Companies Act of the same year.

All this legislation that we are now passing is linked1 up with Bretton Woods. If it had not been for Britain the United States would have been invaded during the first two years of the last war. I do not see why the government should drive the insurance companies into the position of coming to the support of a bank the functioning of which will mean the end of preferences and of freedom of trade and the dissolution of the British empire. It simply means that, so far as we go, we are aiding the government in getting itself out of the great difficulty it got into by passing Bretton Woods. I have been greatly interested in what a financial writer in England, a man of discernment, had to say about the Bretton Woods agreement and what we have done in this parliament, not only in December, 1945, but now. He states:
The proposals are inconsistent, hut the attack on imperial preference and on the very existence of the empire itself is now complete. Chapter 3 provides for the use of quotas to safeguard the balance of payments. Provision for the use of tariffs for this purpose would have afforded recognition of a principal function of imperial preference to maintain effective reciprocity and thereby an equilibrium in the balance of payments. Preferences are to be eliminated but tariffs are merely to be reduced. Most-favoured nation tariff rates are to be lowered to the level of preferential rates. The most-favoured-nation principle is to be applied internally to the countries of the British empire. Universal expansion of production through effective reciprocity is to be sacrificed to American expansionist policy.
What he says is quite true. . We are going even further than the 1911 reciprocity proposals to make this country a hewer of wood and a drawer of water for the United States. This writer continues:	.
Any fiscal concession made by the United (States could be only a token for the American tariff is at such a level as to allow of substantial reduction without impairing its efficiency. No American tariff concession could be genuine unless bilateral action provided for a specific flow of two-way trade. Indeed, to follow the process to its logical conclusion, there would be preferential arrangements independently by each of the states of the American union to the rest of the world. Yet even such action as this would not materially increase the participation of the outside world in the American market because the fiscal policies of the United States have consolidated its internal production and trade and created a highly developed autarchy.
Imperial preference represents a principle which should be inviolate and which should not be open to discussion with any foreign power. Xo concession which can be made 'by any foreign power could compensate for the elimination of imperial preference. In the place of any such surrender, the most-favoured nation clause should be abolished.
I want to read one or two other paragraphs. This is a great writer in the National Review,

Saskatchewan Natural Resources
a paper which along with many others in England, has attacked these proposals. For us to compel these insurance companies- because this is a mandatory act; this is a statute-to make these investments is wrong. The insurance companies are to be compelled to lend your policy money and your trust funds, and the shareholders have been interfered with also. This article goes on to say:
The abrupt termination of lend lease in August, 1945, was the occasion for the opening of negotiations in Washington. On December 6, 1945, an economic and financial agreement was concluded by the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States.
We concluded one a few days later, on December 8, 1945.
The granting of a line of credit by the United States to the United Kingdom follows the clearly defined pattern of United States foreign policy since 1933 evidenced by the Anglo-American trade agreement of 1938, the Atlantic charter, the mutual-aid agreement, the Hot Springs, Bretton Woods and Dumbarton Oaks proposals, the international civil aviation conference and the charter of the united nations. The agreement is determined by the most-favoured nation principle and expansionist policy.
A commercial charter has been distributed and is the basis of an international conference on trade and emploj'ment. The establishment of an international trade organization within the economic and social council of the united nations organization is proposed. The aim is a planned economy and world government.
That is what you are speaking about now.
It is assumed that sacrifices in the common cause were sufficient to warrant the cancellation of the British debt to the United States that arose from the first world war.
They should have been cancelled long ago because Britain protected the shores of the United States.
The benefits received by Britain and the United States in the defeat of their common enemies are deemed to justify the complete and final settlement of lend lease and reciprocal aid in the second world war.
The line of credit is granted exclusively to the United Kingdom and the proceeds will be devoted to purchases in the United States. This constitutes an extreme case of "discrimination" and illustrates the privileged position claimed for money transactions. If the full credit is employed and repayment made over the full fifty-five year period, interest will amount to $2,212,500,000. Repayment could be assured, even at a higher rate of interest, if the proposals for consideration by an international conference on trade and employment were drastically altered.
This is absolutely correct. Why should we go over the heads of the insurance companies and compel them to lend these trust funds to the international bank? I can tell you this: I am surprised that this bill should be introduced in the dying days of this parliament. Certainly it should be considered by the banking and commerce committee, where the insurance companies could be heard. Look at the trouble we got the insurance companies in in 1932. Read the report of the superintendent of insurance with regard to what happened in the United States, and the policy of dealing with common stock, where millions and millions of dollars in trust funds were lost. I say if hon. members will read the report of the superintendent of insurance they will have a different idea of the whole matter.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 and 3 agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported.
