maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT

speechtext: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply) moved the second reading of Bill No. 336, to establish the Canadian maritime commission.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement on second reading?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: I made a complete statement on the resolution, and I think nothing further is required from myself at this time.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
This Bill No. 336 is described as an act to establish the Canadian maritime commission. The official opposition approve the setting up of a maritime commission for Canada. As a matter of fact we have advocated such action for several years; and there are very good reasons for setting up such a commission. For example, there is the importance to Canada of our foreign trade. Then there is the importance of having assured and dependable shipping services. That would include, of course, having the actual shipping, having the merchant seamen to man. the ships, having the men to direct the operation of these shipping activities, and having the facilities for shipbuilding. There is also the importance from the point of view of naval protection. That point was clearly put by one of our senior Canadian naval officers, Admiral Victor Brodeur, who said on November 24, 1943:
It is incorrect .to think that a strong sea power can be obtained by building a strong fighting navy alone. To have real sea power a nation must also have a strong merchant navy.
Those words, I think, will be approved by every hon. member. There is also the importance to Canada of having men in a position to take part in international councils dealing with questions of Shipping. That, too, is an important factor.
You know, Mr. Speaker, Canadians are a maritime race. While very little is said in
this house about maritime questions the fact remains that from the start Canadians have been a maritime people. Take those. Canadians who live on the Atlantic coast. At one time maritimers were the leading shipping men of the world, and they had a Wonderful record both in the actual building of ships and in their operation. Then on the St. Lawrence river we have had a long line of distinguished seamen, largely French-speaking Canadians, who have made a great name as a maritime people. Again, on the great lakes, we have a tradition as a maritime nation. For decades the many ports along those lakes have turned out men interested in ships, even though they did not have the smell of salt water to call them to sea. Of course on the Pacific great interest has always been taken in shipping, and probably it will always remain one of the greatest businesses on that coast. Even on the prairies, where they have only a few large lakes, there is great interest in shipping. It always intrigued me that during the recent war such a large percentage of the men in the Canadian navy should have come from the three prairie provinces; and they made splendid sailors. Time and again references have been made in this house to the type of naval men coming from the prairie provinces. So I repeat that Canadians are a maritime race, and for that reason as well as the others I have given, this bill is of great importance.
The war gave a tremendous impetus to shipping and shipbuilding in Canada; there was a great increase in the interest taken by the people of Canada in shipping; and we now find ourselves with the ships to constitute a merchant navy and with the trained personnel to man them. The other evening the minister gave some interesting figures, which are to be found at page 4203 of Hansard. There he listed the Canadian tonnage at the present time. According to those figures, we have 153 ocean-going ships totalling 982,869 tons. In addition we have eighty ships at present with the British ministry of transport, with a total tonnage of approximately 560,000. I understand that those Ships will be coming back to Canada within a comparatively short space of time. The minister also listed canal freighters and tankers numbering 146, with a total of 285,454 tons. Then he added the west coast passenger boats, sixteen in number, with a total tonnage of 51,235, and the Saint John-Digby ferry with a tonnage of 4,055. This made a total of 316 ocean-going ships in Canada today, totalling 1,323,613 tons, in addition to the eighty ships I referred to previously, now with the British ministry of transport. As

Maritime Commission
hon. members will realize, that is quite a sizeable merchant navy. The minister also gave us some figures with regard to Canadian shipyards; at page 4204, where he said:
The Canadian shipbuilding industry today comprises seventeen major well-equipped shipyards, and there are also, a number of smaller ship and boat building concerns. During the peak of our war effort there were 53,000 men employed on shipbuilding in these major yards alone. Today they have over 16,000 men in their employ . . .
I thought he might have gone on to give us the number of men in the merchant navy, but perhaps he will do that at a later stage in this debate. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I understood that at one time during the war there were about
18,000	men in that service.
In view of these facts it was natural that there should be widespread demands for policies to ensure that we maintain our position as a maritime nation. Those demands have been heard in the House of Commons, not only from members of the opposition, but also from government supporters. I remember that last year the late member for Halifax, Mr. Macdonald, made a plea for the setting up of a maritime commission, and a very fine plea it was. Then there have been demands from union leaders across Canada, leaders of unions interested in the merchant navy. For example, I think most hon. members received a copy of the brief of the Canadian seamen's union entitled "The immediate needs of Canada's shipping industry," and it was a very good brief, too. The shipbuilders have made similar demands. As far back as 1944 they submitted a brief for shipbuilding, with recommendations by the Canadian shipbuilding and ship repairing association. The ship operators have also been in favour of the setting up of a commission. Only this morning I received the 1946 annual of the Canadian Merchant Service Guild. It contains an interesting article headed "Required, a strong government policy". I shall read two paragraphs from the article which is on page 10:
Our dominion government must come forward soon with a strong policy to build up our merchant fleet. We have tihe nucleus of ships and men. Training establishments must be augmented; men encouraged to man our ships in the same way they manned our wartime navy; long-term government assistance must be given to our shipping companies to build modern tonnage.
We have a good fleet of general carriers. We must now 'build tonnage for special routes and trades. Oui government must provide longterm loans to ibuild Canadian flag tonnage on the basis of comparative costs in Canada and elsewhere. We must build passenger ships for our
coastal and offshore trades. We must build refrigerated ships to place our farmers' produce in every foreign market at our pleasure at the time when our farmers will benefit most.
As I have said, there has been a widespread demand for a shipping policy in Canada. The government has not always been in favour of such a policy. Back in 1943 those of us who were interested in establishing a Canadian merchant navy got quite a shock when we read a statement made by the then Minister of Transport, Mr. Michaud. I read the following from a newspaper article of December 24, 1943, in which the then minister is reported as follows:
"I see no future in Canada going into the shipping business on a big scale after the war." The minister told the Canadian press "some of the ships might well ,be used to develop trade between Canada and the West Indies and South America, but to enter competition in trade across the Atlantic and Pacific would be a big undertaking."
In 1943 what I believe was an, interdepartmental committee was set up by the government. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) referred to it the other night when he said, as reported at page 4197 of Hansard:
In October, 1943, the government appointed a special committee to investigate and advise upon future Canadian merchant shipping policy. Two important recommendations of this committee were: that merchant ships should be operated in peacetime by private enterprise; and that all government machinery dealing with merchant shipping should be coordinated. The first of these recommendations has already been fully implemented. The resolution now before the committee seeks to provide the second.
While I assume this was an interdepartmental committee, I believe persons interested in shipping, including representatives of the unions, of shipbuilding firms and1 of ship operators were called in. Apparently that committee have been working for three years. It would be of great help to us if the minister would table the report submitted by them. I should think that report would be worth while, because obviously these men have given shipping and shipbuilding careful consideration. Today however we are not in a position to refer to their recommendations.
Last year the minister was questioned about the setting up of a maritime commission. His statement appears at page 4994 of Hansard where he explained that the present functions with regard to shipping and shipbuilding are being handled by several different departments. Then he went on to say that some progress was being made in the drafting of a maritime act to be administered by a mari-
Maritime Commission

time commission, and promised that legislation would be brought down this year to set up such a commission.
We now have before us the bill setting up the commission. So far as it goes, it is all to the good. But for all practical purposes it does no more. It lays down no policy whatsoever for the development of Canadian shipping and shipbuilding, and for that reason it is a disappointment. It does not implement any policy, and it would seem the government has not yet worked out any policy for the development of Canadian shipping and shipbuilding. Apparently the government is carrying on without a policy, relying on the fact that there is still a demand for the construction of new ships, and also plenty of work for ships now operating. But it will not be long before Canada will have to have a definite shipping and shipbuilding policy.
The functions of the maritime commission, as set out in bill 336, are largely of an advisory nature. They are directed to the studying of various features having to do with shipping and shipbuilding, and the commission is directed to find facts in certain other respects. I submit all that should have been done before this by the interdepartmental committee-* and I have no doubt that to a great extent it has been done. There does not seem to be much reason for setting up a maritime commission merely to carry out another investigation of the whole problem.
It is true that the new commission is given certain minor administrative functions, but those functions are not extensive. For example, the commission is directed on behalf of the Minister of Transport to, exercise and to perform such powers, duties and functions of the minister under the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, as the minister may require. So obviously they are to have some of the administrative functions now exercised by the Minister of Transport. The commission is also directed to administer, in accordance with the regulations of the governor in council, any steamship subventions voted by parliament. That function now comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce. Then it is directed to exercise or perform any other powers, duties or functions conferred1 on or required to be performed by the commission by or pursuant to any other act or order of the governor in council. This last provision is merely a blanket instruction.
I repeat that this bill is only a beginning, and there are certain facts in connection with it which should be considered by the house. In the first place, the bill is in general terms, leaving it to the Minister of Transport to fill in the gaps. Legislation of that kind is

unfair to the house, but we have had a lot of it from the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. I am afraid he has a bad habit of bringing in bills that are merely shells. He sets up the framework, and then reserves to himself, or in this instance to the Minister of Transport, the power to put in all the filling. That is a bad kind of legislation to bring before any legislative chamber.
In the bill the powers and duties of the maritime commission should be clearly defined. It should also set out government policy with respect to shipping and shipbuilding. That has been done in the United States. There they have what is known as the United States maritime commission, which was set up by an act of 1936. At the beginning of the bill establishing that commission wre find this declaration of policy:
It is necessary for the national defence and development of its foreign and domestic commerce that the United States shall have a merchant marine (a) sufficient to carry its domestic water-borne commerce and a substantial portion of the water-borne export and import foreign commerce of the United States and to provide shipping service on all routes essential for maintaining the flow of such domestic and foreign water-borne commerce at all times, (b) capable of serving as a naval and military auxiliary in time of war or national emergency, (c) owned and operated under the United States flag by citizens of the United States in so far as may be practicable, and (d) composed of the best equipped, safest, and most suitable types of vessels, constructed in the United States and manned with a trained and efficient citizen personnel. It is hereby declared to be the policy of the United States to foster the development and encourage the maintenance of such a merchant marine.
We have absolutely no provision of this type in the Canadian bill, nor did the minister define any such policy in his statement the other night on the resolution. He is simply bringing in a skeleton bill setting up a maritime commission. In the United States act we find these duties given to the United States maritime commission:
It shall be the duty of the commission to make a survey of the American merchant marine, as it now exists, to determine what additions and replacements are required to carry forward the national policy declared in section 101 of this act, and the commission is directed to study, perfect, and adopt a long-range programme for replacements and additions to the American merchant marine so that as soon as practicable the following objectives may be accomplished:
First, the creation of an adequate and well balanced merchant fleet, including vessels of all types, to provide shipping service on all routes essential for maintaining the flow of the foreign commerce of the United States, the vessels in sueh fleet to be so designed as to be readily and quickly convertible into transport and supply vessels in a time of national emergency. In planning the development of such a fleet the commission is directed to cooperate closely with

Maritime Commission
the navy department as to national defence needs and the possible speedy adaptation of the merchant fleet to national defence requirements.
Second, the ownership and the operation of such a merchant fleet by citizens of the United States in so far as may be practicable.
Third, the planning of vessels designed to afford the best and most complete protection for passengers and crew against fire and all marine perils.
Another point about the present bill is that it does not coordinate all government machinery. The understanding given to us the other evening was that the bill would coordinate all government machinery having to do with shipping and shipbuilding. The bill simply refers to some of the functions to be performed under the Canada Shipping Act and to the subventions. The minister knows that there are many other governmental activities having to do with shipping and shipbuilding.
In the third place, there is nothing in the bill about replacing ships as they become obsolete or of making additions to our merchant fleet or keeping the fleet up to date. We may have a good merchant fleet at the present time, but it is not going to be up to date for very long. Other maritime nations are constantly making improvements in their vessels and we cannot be satisfied with the fleet as it was during the war. There must be some provision made for keeping our merchant fleet modern.
For example, there is the question of types. How are we to get the new types of ships in Canada? The United States dealt with that problem in their bill setting up the United States maritime commission. They made provision for the setting up of a fund for the replacement of ships and sooner or later Canada will have to do something along that line. As I say, there is no provision whatever for it in the present bill.
There is nothing in the bill either for the protection or training of merchant seamen. The United States have a provision in their bill, and I quote from section 301 (a):
The commission is authorized and directed to investigate the employment and wage conditions in ocean-going shipping and, after making such investigation and after appropriate hearings, to incorporate in the contracts authorized under titles VI and VII of this act minimum-manning scales and minimum-wage scales and reasonable working conditions for all officers and crews employed on all types of vessels receiving an operating-differential subsidy.
There are further provisions in that particular part of their act having to do with merchant seamen. There is also provision for two kinds of subsidies. First of all, for what they call the construction-differential subsidy; provisions are laid down at some length for
subsidizing the construction of ships. There is no such provision in the Canadian bill. Then the United States provide for an oper-ating^differential subsidy. It may be that Canada under her subventions and subsidies policy has much the same feature, but it is not set out in the bill. At the present time subventions come under the Department of Trade and Commerce. There is no explanation of how Canada is to subsidize the operation of her ships or whether or not she is to do it at all.
The United States have another interesting provision in their act under the heading of "Private charter operation." Their commission is given the power, if it is necessary, to build ships and to construct them where they wish. Section 702 reads:
The commission is authorized to have constructed in domestic yards, on the Atlantic and gulf and Pacific coasts, such new vessels as it shall determine may be required to carry out the objects of this >a.ct, hikI to hxive old vessels reconditioned or remodeled in such yards: provided, that if satisfactory contracts for such new construction or reconstruction, in accordance with the provisions of this act, cannot be obtained from private shipbuilders, the commission is authorized to have such vessels constructed, reconditioned, or remodeled in United States navy yards.
In the Canadian bill there is nothing whatever about placing shipbuilding work in different parts of Canada. Apparently the government has no policy with regard to * having shipbuilding done, say in the maritimes or on the Pacific. There is no provision whatever for diverting traffic through Canadian ports, instead of having it go through United States ports as has been happening in recent months. There is no indication as to whether it is government policy to restrict coastal trade to Canadian vessels.
I repeat, the bill is a framework. I think it must be described as a shell and largely window-dressing. Perhaps it was intended to cover up the fact that the government has no policy whatever.

It has some ships; that is
better than having a policy.

speechtext:
We had a hard time to
persuade the minister to build the ships. Apparently this bill is the best we can get at the present time. I hope it will be improved before very long. I would urge upon the minister that he take certain actions in connection with the bill. For example, I suggest that practical men be put on the commission which is to be composed of three members. It would seem reasonable that there should be a man who understands the labour point of view, a man who understands the out-
Maritime Commission

look of the shipbuilders and another who understands the outlook of the ship operators. Perhaps it would be well to have the views of these groups as to nominations for membership on the commission.
A very good feature of the bill is the one providing for advisory committees. I am not quite clear, from reading the bill, whether it is the intention to have an advisory committee in the maritimes, another on the St. Lawrence, another on the great lakes and one on the Pacific coast, or whether the advisory committees are. to be made up of representatives from labour, shipbuilding and ship operators. But any rate I think it is a very wise plan to have these advisory committees.
The 'bill makes provision for the hiring of personnel. Apparently what the explanatory note describes as "regular officers, clerks and employees" are to be civil servants, but whether the word "regular" means only the small-paid jobs or just what it does mean is not clear. There is provision in the bill foi the commission to engage direct professions and technical advisers and assistants. The minister should give consideration to having all of the personnel employed through the civil service commission, which has been bypassed far too often in legislation enacted in the last few years.
I would urge the minister not to insist upon setting up this maritime commission as a crown company. I pointed out earlier that its functions are largely advisory, with certain minor administrative duties, but I do not think these duties go beyond those carried out by many departmental branches. This commission seems to resemble the air transport board which was set up two or three years ago and was not set up as a crown corporation. I would urge that the minister keep this commission, for the time being at least, as a branch of the Department of Transport, thereby keeping it much more closely under parliamentary supervision.
The other evening the minister was asked, during the discussion on the resolution preceding the bill to establish a dominion coal board, why it was that he was setting up that board as a crown corporation, and I thought his reasons were not very good. They were in fact rather amusing. The minister gave this explanation at page 4249 of Hansard:
My hon. friend asked why this commission should take the form of a corporation. I shall have to get a more satisfactory answer to that question than I can give offhand. All I can say is that for a commission to operate and do business it seems to be necessary that they be formed into a corporation. All the commissions I know of that operate around Ottawa are formed into corporations;-

There are quite a few that are not. The minister went on:
-for example, the national research council is a corporation; as is the national harbours board.
The national harbours board owns property all over the country and has far more widespread operations than this commission will have. The minister went on:
I could mention others. I do not know why, other than that a corporation is a convenient form. It provides convenience of accounting and an accepted pattern for doing business that is lacking when three men simply form themselves into a committee.
You see, Mr. Speaker, companies in Canada are organized to do business, not to perform functions of government, but the minister seems to have forgotten that fact. Every year more of these crown companies are being launched, They are like small planets breaking off from the sun and the minister is the champion planet launcher in the cabinet. Certainly, if the government is to persist in establishing these crown companies we must have a committee of this house whose duty it will be to act as watchdog on these crown companies.

Mr. Speaker, when this bill was before the house last week, the minister, if I remember correctly, stated that there were 16,000 men employed in our shipbuilding yards and that they had orders in hand for 122 various ships, which total, roughly, 300,000 gross tons. He went on to say:
The fact of the matter is that every major shipyard in Canada has all the work which it can do for the next twelve or eighteen months, which is a situation that I hope the maritime commission will be able to maintain over the years as the Department of Reconstruction has been able to maintain it over the past five or six years.
I asked the minister at that time if he could tell us where the 122 ships were being built or would be built and how many men were employed in each of our shipbuilding yards. He told me at that time that since I lived in Saint John, where the only major New Brunswick shipyard is located, I should be able to tell him the number of men employed there, and, I presume, the number of ships being built. I have no information as to the number of ships being built or the number of men employed in shipbuilding in the province of Nova Scotia. The minister went on:
I will try to give that information when the bill is being discussed.
Could the minister now tell us where the 122 ships are being built or will be built and how many men are employed in each of the

Maritime Commission
major shipyards? When the minister said, "The fact of the matter is that every major shipyard in Canada has all the work which it can do for the next twelve or eighteen months," I should like to tell him that from the inquiries I have made at the shipbuilding yard in the port of Saint John, which he says is one of the major yards, no ships are being built there at the present time.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) has pointed out that this bill sets up a maritime commission but does not announce any policy. Indeed it admits that the government has no specific policy for the maintenance of Canadian steel shipbuilding in the post-war years. This is so, despite the fact that we have heard so much of a maritime commission bill in the past year, and despite the fact that all those in Canada interested in shipbuilding expected great things from the bill and from the minister. I think they will be sadly disappointed by the complete absence of any policy in the bill. This is another government promise without any performance. It is the kind of promise that can be evaded very easily when it comes to taking steps to implement it in the future. It looks to me as though this will be another case where this government will act one or two or three years too late in setting up a policy to cope with this problem, which will be a great problem if we are to maintain 16,000 people employed in the shipyards in peace time after the present war-stimulated demand for ships has lessened.
I am very apprehensive that we shall find that shipbuilding will be treated in the same way as housing, defence and immigration have been treated. We sliall find that, whatever policy is finally put into effect, it will be a little too late. Even though it may be a good policy, it will be too late to have its proper and full effect to carry out the purpose for which it was intended. To my mind, matters of this kind depend so much for their success upon them being ready and launched in time. In 1947, two years after the war, the government, having failed to produce a policy to ensure that steel shipbuilding will continue in Canada in the post-war years, is keeping shipyards and dhip operators, and those who work in these shipyards, in a state of uncertainty over the future. There is nothing like uncertainty to create inefficiency and to dry up an industry. Unless, therefore, continuity between the present demand for ships and shipbuilding and the * demand in future years is assured by a policy which will carry from the reconversion period into peace,
there is considerable danger that we shall lose t'he steel shipbuilding industry in this country, an industry of which the minister has many times said, and rightly said, that he is proud.
We do not find in the sections of the bill any determination of many points of policy that are well known to the minister and to everyone who has studied the matter. Thus even if that commission gets going now we cannot have any recommendations they might make implemented until 1948 at the earliest, when the act could be amended, and probably not until 1949. That will be three or four years after the end of the war. When we bear in mind that it takes about two years to build a ship from the time it is originally decided to build it, it may well be that we shall be past the time when there is a demand throughout the world for shipbuilding facilities, and that Canadians engaged in the shipping trade, who have no assurance from the government as to what the future of the trade will be, will have to forget their natural inclinations to deal in Canada, and go elsewhere to place their orders for ships, getting the best terms they can.
This commission is set up to perform, under the Canada Shipping Act, certain duties which somebody else is now doing; to administer subsidies which are now being paid by some other department of government; to make investigations which, I believe, have already been made to a considerable extent and Which certainly dhould have been made by the officials of the Department of Transport in the past. One of its chief purposes, too, is to make a policy which the government should have made years ago. I think that people interested in this business have considerable cause for alarm. When I say that, I am not unmindful of the fact that everyone expected a much more definite and forward policy than this.
I want to ask the minister, when he replies, to tell us why we could not have that longterm policy for the maintenance of a steel shipbuilding industry in Canada now. The member for Vancouver South referred to what the minister said, as reported at page 4197 of Hansard, about the interdepartmental committee on shipbuilding which was set up in 1943, and which reported, I presume, within a year or so from that date. They must have made recommendations as to what would be required if we were to keep the industry in Canada. Great Britain, the United States and Australia have all announced their policies; those in United States and Great Britain were announced before the war, and
Maritime Commission

Australia's in the summer of 1945. They know definitely what they will do, but again, Canada does not know.
I would ask the minister why there is this delay in announcing a policy. I would point out to the house that the establishment of the broad lines of any shipbuilding policy does not require any basic research. We have ample examples of what can be done and what has been done in practice in other countries, and in other countries which have the same system of government as ours and the same problems and needs. The United States maritime commission administers restrictions on coastwise trade; the retirement of old vessels, and their scrapping or sale abroad in order to keep the merchant fleet modern; and already, even since the war, some of the old United States ships have been sold into Canada. I understand that two which are forty-six years old came under the Canadian flag in 1945. These old ships are not the kind we should have in our merchant marine.
If you look at the history between the wars you find that many United States ships were sold into the Canadian trade, more than were constructed in Canada, and again these ships were brought from the United States when they were very old. While I do not know this of my own knowledge, I would not be surprised if some of these ships had been sold from under the American flag by reason of the policies of the United States maritime commission.
I suggest that there is not a great deal of time to wait before deciding whether we shall allow other countries with a maritime policy to dump old ships on us or to compete with us by means of special assistance.
In Great Britain, the British shipping assistance act was passed in 1939. Under that act a definite policy of loans and grants for the construction and operation of tramp steamers was provided, and in particular a "liner defence committee" was set up which had the specific purpose of administering subsidies in the construction and operation of liners, if these liners were meeting foreign subsidized competition, and not otherwise.
The minister, at page 4209 of Hansard, in his remarks in the resolution stage, was asked by the hon. member for Vancouver South whether it was government policy to subsidize shipbuilding in Canada. I wonder what the minister meant by saying, "No, not at the present time"? It seems to suggest that at some time in the future he might be considering subsidizing ship construction in Canada. Then again, if that is his intention, I say, why leave the matter in doubt? Why leave it uncertain? It is all very well to say that the shipyards have a considerable number of orders on hand at the present time, but that will not continue indefinitely. Delay in the determination of this important question can do a great deal of damage.
Earlier in his statement, and referring to the duty of the commission, the minister said, as reported at page 4209 of Hansard, that it will be its duty:
... to recommend such incentives as may be needed to induce private industry to build a different type of ship or to modernize its fleet; and certainly it will be. the function of the commission to advise the minister of any steps that should be taken to stimulate Shipbuilding in Canada and make it competitive with shipbuilding in other countries.
I want to urge the minister to make very sure that he take those steps in time, if he is to take them at all; I think this government has given us plenty of evidence on the other matters I have mentioned, such as housing and immigration, that it is not always inclined to do things in time. If we are to maintain steel shipbuilding in Canada, we must depend primarily upon our own shipowners and operators to provide the solid core of any continuing shipbuilding business. Those operators are not catered to at all in this bill. They must know the conditions they face if they are to make their commitments far enough in advance. If they are to assume that there is no government policy, they will be obliged to look around and shop in world markets and to make sure that they protect themselves adequately against possible recessions in business in the future. If, as is quite commonly talked of and practised, I believe, in many' maritime countries, there are to be any special considerations given to those shipowners in order that they may build up funds wherewith to build new ships in Canada, the longer that policy is delayed, the less able will be those shipowners to carry on in the face of bitter competition, which may arise in future years.
In Canada our shipbuilding is under the competitive disadvantage that our wage scales are high and we have not a long history of steel shipbuilding behind us so that we may produce with much greater efficiency than other countries. If the minister really intends that there shall be a continuing industry in Canada, I am sure there is nothing which could be more important than that the industry and the people working in, it should have the assurance that they can go into it,

Maritime Commission
improve their methods, and be secure for some time ahead in the carrying on of that business and making it competitive with that of other countries.
Another thing which I consider would cater to the continuation of the industry, and which,
1 understand, is not now being done, is the making available to the shipyards of an adequate supply of steel. I am well aware that the minister has difficulties in dishing out steel to everyone in Canada who needs it, but I understand that the present allotment of steel to shipyards is not sufficient to enable them to gain the greatest efficiency of effort and to meet delivery dates as certainly as they might otherwise be able to do. Without criticizing the minister's policy in this respeqt, I suggest to him that one thing which could be done to keep the shipyards in operation for a long time in the future, would be to make sure that they get enough materials so that they may accept orders which are coming to Canada in these times of great demand and build up a reputation around the world for Canadian ships and for meeting delivery dates certainly.
I cannot help feeling that this bill which was brought in with a great deal of eclat and grand references-and most proper ones-to the good; job done by the Canadian merchant fleet during the war, could be just a stall, although I am not saying it is. It could be that the government is talking big, but is really hedging its bets on whether or not we are to have a continuing shipbuilding industry in Canada. That doubt will remain in my mind until the government has said yes or no to the definite principles which have been followed by other countries in the development and maintenance of their shipbuilding and ship operation programme.
Mr. ANGUS MacINNIS (Vancouver East); I hesitate to speak on this bill because, from reading it, I was not clear as to its ultimate purpose. The minister may have it -all worked out as to what the functions of the maritime commission are to be and how it will fit into the Canadian shipbuilding industry, but at -the moment I do not think it is clear in the bill. On the other hand, I am equally in the dark after listening to my two hon. friends from Vancouver. I do not know exactly what they want. Do they want the government to subsidize shipbuilding? Perhaps that would be a risky business at this moment. I do not know. However, in my opinion, if the government is to have a definite shipping programme, it is inevitable that it should go into the shipbuilding and ship operating
business and do it for the economic benefit of Canada, without insisting that it pay its own way at all times.
I was not in the house when the minister made his statement in moving the resolution, but I read what he said at that time.
It is interesting to note what happened following the first great war; because if we have not a programme somewhat different from the programme we had at that time the same thing is likely to happen now. I should like to read a very short paragraph from the minister's statement, at page 4195 of Hansard. He pointed out that as at 1919 the government owned some sixty-three ships; then he said;
The entire fleet therefore only commenced to earn revenue after the armistice; and by the time all the ships were in service the post-war boom in shipping was over -and freight rates had dropped more than fifty per cent. The cost to build this fleet at the peak of shipyard prices was approximately $80 million.
If on this occasion the government-owned ships had not been disposed of earlier than was the case on the former occasion, the government might have been able to take advantage of the high shipping rates and the good business now available. It is interesting to study the statistics of shipbuilding and ship repairing in Canada between world war I and world war II; that is between 1917 and 1942. Statistics on the subject can be found in the brief prepared by the shipbuilding and ship repairing association and referred to this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). On page 42 it contains a table which shows that the high peak following the first war was in 1919, when there were in Canada seventy-eight establishments; the gross value of products was S186,500,000, in round figures; salaried employees numbered 1.384 and wage employees 22,318, with wages of approximately $27,000,000. Then activity began to drop, so that by 1933, which was the low year, there were thirty-eight establishments; the gross value of the product was only $4,521,000; salaried employees numbered only 369, and manual employees, 1,885, with a total annual wage of $1,964,000. The shipbuilding and ship repairing industry just disappeared, and- that was only a few years before the beginning of world war II. Then it began to go up again, until in 1942 there were seventy-nine establishments with a gross value of product of $242,000,000; salaried employees numbering 2,868, and manual or wage employees numbering 47,264, with total wages of over $87,000,000. I do not know the number of workers today, but I think someone said there were 18.000. Nor do I know the gross value of the product;
Maritime Commission

but unless there is a demand for shipping which will make the operation of ships a profitable venture for private enterprise, there will be no shipbuilding; and unless my friends are willing to have the government go into shipbuilding itself, I do not see that there is any other policy that will produce ships.
I intend to reserve anything further I have to say until we are in committee and the functions of the maritime commission becomes clear. However, since labour employed on the ships and in building the ships has an interest in the shipping business of this country, I would1 suggest that the minister give consideration to having labour represented on this commission, so that there may be cooperation between all factors connected with the industry.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
I have listened with interest to the debate on the second reading of this bill. It seems to me the principal complaint is that in drafting this bill we have not attempted to usurp the functions of parliament. All matters covered by the bill are functions being performed by government agencies at the present time. The purpose of the bill is to correlate those agencies and gradually to bring them under a single directing force.
The bill seeks to set up an authoritative body to advise the government on shipping and shipbuilding matters and to administer certain matters relating to those industries. The proposed commission is to consist of three full-time officials who, as a body corporate, will be responsible to and subject to the direction of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). I might explain that there is nothing sinister about the form of organization known as a body corporate. It should not be confused with the crown companies set up under the Companies Act of Canada, for which provision was made in a bill passed by the last parliament. It is simply declared a corporation in drafting the act, and functions as a corporation. The purpose is merely to bring three men together so that in their executive work they may function as an entity. The commission will be staffed by the civil service commission in the usual manner, and that is a clause I would hardly expect to be criticized by anyone. There is provision that with the approval of the governor in council the commission may employ professional and technical advisers and assistants for temporary periods and for specific work.

Obviously occasions may arise when it will be necessary to employ people with special knowledge to perform special duties for temporary periods.
The function of the commission in its advisory capacity is to consider and recommend to the minister such policies and measures as it considers necessary for the operation, maintenance, manning and development of a merchant marine and a shipbuilding and ship repairing industry, commensurate with our maritime needs. It seems to me that statement of functions is comprehensive, and in accordance with the desires of those who have spoken in this debate. In order to fulfil this function, the commission will have to ascertain and record a number of matters concerning our own industries and those of other nations. On its administrative side it is intended that it shall act on behalf of the minister in dealing with certain responsibilities which are vested in him by the Canada Shipping Act, 1934. It will also absorb the duties now performed by the steamship subsidies section of the Department of Trade and Commerce. It will be available to absorb other suitable administrative duties which may be allotted to it from time to time.
The expenses of the commission will be paid from appropriations duly authorized by parliament, and the commission will render an annual report of its activities to parliament through the Minister of Transport.
I might point out that all the policies of the commission will require to be approved by parliament, because the only funds which will be available to the commission to carry out its policies will be those funds voted by parliament from time to time.
In drafting the bill, we have endeavoured to provide in the commission a ready and accessible point of contact between the government and all sections of the shipping and shipbuilding industries. In this connection, hon. members will note that a special reference is made to the setting up of advisory committees by the commission, which will enable it to obtain all the points of view of the parties concerned in any particular matter.
It is our thought, amongst others, that a standing advisory committee consisting of representatives of ship operators, shipbuilders, 'and seafaring personnel should be set up as soon as possible, which will provide a forum for discussion on a number of matters concerning the efficiency and development of the industries.
There is also a need today for a well-informed government agency to represent the nation's views in various international shipping

Maritime Commission
matters which from time to time are called into discussion by the united nations and related organizations.
In short, Mr. Speaker, the government is of the opinion, that the setting up of an organization directly concerned with Canadian shipping and shipbuilding problems is now desirable. One of its functions will be to assume responsibility for any continuing government-owned merchant, ships now being operated through the agency of Park Steamship Company, Limited.
In moving the second, reading of the bill, I would again emphasize that we seek from its provisions cooperation with private enterprise but not control of it. The bill does not represent any change in the policy which we have previously adopted., but provides only what we believe and hope will be a more up-to-date medium for carrying out that policy.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) mentioned that we are a maritime people. I agree; Canadians take to the sea naturally, and this will provide an outlet for the aspirations of our people in that direction. He mentioned that during the war our merchant marine reached a peak of 18,000 Canadian seamen. The publication from which the hon. member quoted, the 1946 Year Book of the Canadian merchant service guild, mentions that at March 31, 1946, there were
12,000	Canadian seamen employed on Canadian ships. The last tabulation of the Department of Labour indicates that about 14,000 Canadian seamen are employed on Canadian ships at the present time.
The suggestion was made that we should freeze government policy. It is felt that by doing so we would bring more security into the lives of Canadian workers. I suggest that if we were to freeze government policy at this day, the policy would be to say that the shipbuilding fraternity and ship operating fraternity are doing exceedingly well, and are well able to look after themselves. Earnings in both branches of the industry at the present time are abnormally high. I know of no feeling of uncertainty in the minds of those engaged in the industry. It seems to me the greatest peril they have to face is that there might be a change of government in this country. But since there is no indication of that on the horizon, it seems to me that both branches of the industry can proceed, with reasonable security, and that the government which has brought the industry to its present satisfactory position will be able to look after it in the future.
