speechtext:
Well, I should relieve their worries as much as possible when I speak at this time.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) has compared the present situation with that after the last great war. He suggested that the same result is inevitable. I would point out the difference between the position after this war and that after the last one. The first difference is that the shipbuilding programme of the first great war was undertaken in 1918 and finished, I believe, in 1921. In other words, it was not a wartime shipbuilding programme; it was a postwar shipbuilding programme. Then the ships were carried at their construction costs, and the construction costs of a high-cost period. In the present instance our present fleet of ships was built during the war. True, they were built in a period of rising costs, nevertheless the great bulk of the fleet was built under cost levels which today look very reasonable indeed.
The policy has been to dispose of the ships to private interests, and I would point out another substantial difference: the ships were not disposed of to private interests at their cost price. They were disposed of to private interests at a price which a committee of experts believed represented the level at which the ships might profitably be operated in the future.
The suggestion has been made that there should be provision for a replacement fund. Provision has been made for a replacement fund. These ships were sold under arrangements which provided for double depreciation, and also provided that in the first year of operation there could be an additional writeoff of thirteen per cent of the cost. In other word^, the ships could be written off at twenty-five per cent of their cost in the first year, and at twelve per cent of their cost for each succeeding year. The result of that provision will be that the money invested in the ships can be recovered within a reasonable period of time, and the funds recovered can be made available to finance a ship replacement programme.
Then it has been suggested that there should be provision in the bill for protection and training of seamen. I point out to hon.
Maritime Commission

members that existing legislation makes ample provision for the protection and training of seamen. The commission will, of course, examine existing legislation, correlate it, and recommend to the government any changes in existing legislation which should be made from time to time, for the purpose of strengthening the over-all legislation in any particular.
To sum up, the bill provides a framework for coordinating the work of all government departments which have to do with shipbuilding or ship operating. It will provide a new approach to the problems of the future. Practical men will have an opportunity of making recommendations to the government which will be useful in meeting new developments in the industry; and at each session parliament will be able to review the work of the board and to implement such recommendations as the government -feels are desirable to cope with the future of the industry.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
What would be likely to
happen if the commission were to report to the administration that, for instance, there was a scarcity of facilities for the building of ships, that marine insurance was too high, or something of that kind? How would the government proceed to take care of that? Would they undertake to build dry docks at the expense of the government, or would they command those now in the business to expand their facilities?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
There are ample provisions today in the law to take care of the situations to which my hon. friend has referred. There is the federal Dry Docks Subsidies Act administered by the Department of Public Works, under which any body of men who desire to build a dry dock can approach the government for subsidy assistance. Means could be found to implement any recommendation of the commission, whether for the enlargement of shipbuilding activities or to enlarge or improve the fleet. Almost any recommendation that I can think of could be handled by the existing law.
The hon. member for St. John-Albert asked about shipbuilding in the maritimes. I have some figures here showing the number employed in shipyards in the maritimes:
March	 3,219
April	 3,090
May	 2,990
The figures for the whole of Canada are as follows:
March	 16,820
April	 17.489
May	   18,202

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: The trend there is entirely different from that in the maritimes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Let us be sensible about this. Employment in shipyards fluctuates owing to the stage of each shipyard's programme. For example, at Halifax they are in the process of finishing two destroyers and they have just undertaken to build three ships for Argentina at a cost of $7,000,000. In the interval men are doing repair work. The best employer is a combination of the two, shipbuilding and repair work, but certain yards prefer to specialize on repair work, and I understand that that is the situation at Saint John. These yards are operated privately, and all I can say is that there is so much shipbuilding work offering around the world that anyone who really looks for that type of work cannot help but find all he cares to undertake. That is all I can say about shipbuilding in the maritime provinces, and I think this covers all I have to say on second reading.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Could the minister fable the report of the intergovernmental committee which investigated this whole question of shipping and shipbuilding?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: No, it was a private report.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: It is a confidential report?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: AH reports from civil servants to their ministers are confidential.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Were people engaged in the industry called in, in connection with the work of that committee?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: The committee was made up of civil servants and it took evidence from witnesses from the trade.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Definitions.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Why is the set-up here so different from the United States maritime commission?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Two different forms of government and two different legislative bodies are concerned. I cannot think of any reason why it should be the same.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Corporation established.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
This section provides that the commission may enter into contracts on behalf of His Majesty, but there is no pro-

Maritime Commission
vision for the commission to make contracts on its own behalf or to sue or be sued. Is it intended that the commisison acting in the capacity of time charterer for one of the Park steamship vessels could be sued by the other party?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: No. The commission can contract only in the name of His Majesty. It is like a government department, which I understand to be the form my hon. friend advocates.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Officers, clerks and employees.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Why is it not possible to get technical and professional men through the civil service commission?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: The method employed by the civil service commission is to advertise for two months and then have a board examine the applicants and report. It takes usually six months to get a senior officer through the civil service commission. The maritime commission could hardly wait that long in the case of an emergency. My hon. friend has spoken of flexibility and speed in making decisions to meet emergencies. For instance, someone has said that one great problem in the shipbuilding industry is to get sufficient steel. Would my hon. friend suggest that they meet that problem by applying to the civil service commission for a steel expert?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
The commission do not
supply steel. What has that to do with the civil service commission?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: My hon. friend suggests a provision that they should not get technical help except through the commission, but I think it would be rather hopeless if they had a situation of that kind and had to rely upon the commission for help.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: If it takes the civil service commission six months to get technical or professional men, perhaps some changes should be made in the administration. Will any of the professional or technical men engaged by the maritime commission be engaged through the civil service commission?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: They will be if they are permanent employees, but not necessarily if they are employed for a temporary period.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: It says, "or for specific work."

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Specialized, short-term jobs.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
I am wondering about the meaning of "temporary." There are many
civil servants who have been temporary from youth to old age, but I would not suppose that "temporary" as used here would apply to such civil servants. I would be inclined to agree that for short periods of time and for temporary purposes we should not insist that they be selected by the civil service commission, but if they are to be just called temporary employees and carried on the staff, as a large percentage of employees now are, I think they should be recruited through the civil service commission.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: My hon. friend is thinking of temporary men while the bill is referring to a temporary period. The purpose is that men engaged for temporary periods will be employed outside of the civil service commission.

Section agreed to.
Sections 5 and 6 agreed to.
On section 7-Powers of commission.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: I have been informed that one of the bottlenecks in the shipbuilding industry is the lack of designers. I presume that that will be covered by the investigators carried on by this commission.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Some progress has been made toward correcting that situation. It was a serious lack in the early days of the war, but shipbuilders have formed themselves into an association and have arranged to exchange and pool talent in designing ships. There is now an exchange of designers between the yards, and efforts will continue to be made to build up the strength of Canada's designing staffs.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: The minister, in his explanation of the bill, said that Park steamships to a large extent stopped the transference of ships to foreign registry. Will this commission be given the power to stop the transference of ships to foreign registry? Suppose a ship is outfitting in Vancouver and it decides to register in Panama and to import men to man the boat. That boat should be manned by Canadian seamen since it is being outfitted in a Canadian port. Will the commission be given power to do what was done to a large extent with Park Steamships?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Every ship that was sold by Park Steamships to Canadians was sold with the proviso that the owner could not apply to the government for a change of registry. That takes care of that situation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
For how
long?
Maritime Commission

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: For an indefinite period. The board will have power to advise the minister whether to permit change of registry or not and will advise the minister with regard to admitting foreign ships to Canadian register. Provision is already made in our legislation covering the latter point; provision was made in the sale of the ships to cover the first point, and neither will in future be acted on by the minister, I would assume, without the advice of the maritime commission.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Will the recommendations made by the commission be available to parliament? Provision is made here for the commission to make recommendations on various aspects of shipping and shipbuilding policy. Will parliament have an opportunity of seeing those recommendations?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: The commission are civil servants under a minister and therefore their recommendations to the minister will be privileged, as is the case with all recommendations of civil servants to ministers.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Provision is also made for the commission to examine into, ascertain and keep records on various matters, including the type, size, speed and other requirements of the vessels which, in the opinion of the commission, should be employed. Once it has made that investigation, has the commission power to do anything about the matter, or has the government power to do anything about it so that we can have the right type of ships built?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Such matters involve money. If the government believes that a certain type of ship is desirable, and1 the shipbuilders will not build it without assistance, the commission can recommend to the minister that provision be made to grant the required assistance and the minister can bring an estimate before parliament. If parliament approves, the assistance can be given.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: That is the scheme the minister has in mind, that if the commission recommends that faster ships be built in Canada the shipbuilding firms will be paid whatever is required to produce those ships?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: I might point out that, in deference to the opposition and to confirm with about half the speeches I have heard in this parliament, I have taken great care to see that parliament is in complete control so far as aid to shipping is concerned.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: The minister is learning at last.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
Section 7 does not refer in terms to any government vessels. What

power will the maritime commission have in respect of vessels owned by the Canadian government which are not engaged in ordinary commercial trade? Would the establishment of a coastguard come within the purview of the commission?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: In matters of that kind the commission will have just the powers that the minister agrees to delegate to it from time to time.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Is power given to the commission to allocate shipbuilding, to 'have it carried on in one part of the country or in another part?	.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: A vexed question concerns foreign ships engaged in our coastwise trade. Will the commission have power to advise on that?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Under existing law, foreign ships are prohibited from engaging in coastwise trade.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: I mean ships other than Canadian-built ships.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Any provision of that kind is a matter of government policy. The commission will have the opportunity of expressing its views to the minister, and the minister will require action by parliament to change the existing situation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Would it be the duty of the commission to make recommendations on that kind of matter without specific orders from the minister?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Certainly. The commission will be expected to recommend any measure which in its opinion will improve the position of ship operations and shipbuilding, but whether the minister and the government accept their recommendations is for the latter to decide.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Skeena first raised the question he referred to this afternoon several months ago and the position is still tangled. Park steamships were being sold in the United States; United States crews were taking those ships to Canadian ports and being discharged, and Chinese crews were imported to man those ships under foreign registry and then were allowed to sail to Canadian ports. When this matter was first raised it was referred to immigration, to ascertain whether under our immigration regulations crews could be brought into Canada and allowed to sail on Canadian ships. The matter was not cleared up to my satis-

Maritime Commission
faction, and the point raised iby the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard is whether it would be the function of this commission to see to it that Canadian ships sailing from Canadian ports would be manned by Canadian crews. Section 7 seemed to give the commission a good deal of latitude, and if they exercise that latitude they could eliminate the grievance raised by the two Vancouver members. Could the minister be specific on that question as to whether the commission would have the function of determining the crews that would sail from Canada on Canadian ships?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: My hon. friend is raising an issue that is not realistic. The records of the Park Steamship Company indicate that no ship was sold to United States interests, with two exceptions. Two very badly damaged ships, which Park steamships believed should be sold in the damaged condition rather than repaired, for reasons of prudent economy, were thus disposed of; but there were no serviceable ships sold to United States interests. As to what became of those two ships, I have no information. The Canada Shipping Act governs the employment of seamen on Canadian ships, and it will be the duty of the maritime commission to examine that act and to recommend any changes which, in its opinion, would strengthen and improve the act and bring about an improvement in conditions.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
That still does not answer the question. It may be true that Park steamships have not sold ships in the United States, but is it true that American ships can be manned by American seamen, come into Canadian ports where the American seamen are discharged, the ship put under Panamanian registry, and sail from Canada being manned by Chinese or imported seamen? That complaint has been made specifically by the Canadian seamen's union. It is well known to many members of the house. The matter was raised about three months ago and was referred to the immigration authorities and we were assured by them that it was not in accordance with their regulations.
All I want to be clear about is this. If this maritime commission, which is a desirable one, and something that we have been advocating for a considerable time, is to have supreme jurisdiction in regulating the crews that will be sailing on Canadian ships from Canadian ports, and determining also conditions and so forth, so that we may get away from this bootlegging system which has developed since the close of the war. whereby
ships are sold and the merchant marine services in different countries are scrapped, thereby getting around our regulations in the manner disclosed in this house, then I am satisfied. A United States crew comes in on a ship. That crew is discharged and the ship is then manned by an imported crew under Panamanian registry and is allowed to sail.
During the war we had considerable difficulty, in the earlier stages at least, when scrap was prohibited from leaving the United States to go to any other country. They would clear from the United States and come to a Canadian port where the crew could be discharged and another crew put on board, and so they could clear from Canada to Japan and deliver scrap to that country, which scrap was later used against ourselves. From discussions I have heard, and from a brief which I read from the seamen's union, that kind of thing is going on again, to the detriment of the development of our own merchant service and our own seamen as well as to the detriment of the British merchant service. Some United States interests are developing a bootlegging system whereby they can get cheap labour. When they cannot clear from a United States port under other conditions they get around their own regulations by clearing from a port in Canada. If this commission has power to stop that, I am satisfied with the clause.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: The section does not give the commission any authority to enforce or to establish. It merely says that it may examine into, ascertain and keep records of and advise any such authority as was suggested by the member for Cape Breton South. Perhaps the power is contained in the next section.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
My hon. friend is correct. There are existing statutes covering the points raised. It is the duty of the commission to examine into those statutes and recommend improvements in them in order to carry out the purpose intended, and to submit such recommendations to the minister for his action in obtaining appropriate legislation. A United States ship is under the supervision of the United States government. It can come to Canadian ports for certain purposes, but one of the purposes is not to discharge the crew. If the crew deserts, then the deserters are sent back to the countries from which they came; but certainly, under any law of Canada, the captain could not discharge the crew in a Canadian port and take on a different crew. The action of the ship is governed by the law of the country whose flag the ship flies. As far
Maritime Commission

as immigration is concerned, there are certain actions which this country does not allow, and if there are any infractions it will be the duty of the maritime commission to bring them to the attention of the appropriate minister to see that they do not continue.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: A hull was taken out of the port of Seattle, manned by a United States crew, brought to Vancouver and outfitted in the drjr dock there, andt the owners told1 the seafarers international union, "We wall put this vessel under Panamanian registry and import a crew and put that crew on."

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: That may be so, but the ship was a United States vessel. It never at any time, I take it, 'became a Canadian ship.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: The point is that it is under Canadian jurisdiction while it is in our port, and we should not be responsible, for pulling off fast ones such as that. I read a report from London which indicated that there is a world ship racket at the present time to put hulls under Panamanian registry where there are no maritime laws at all.

Section agreed to.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at seven o'clock.
On section 8-Duties of commission.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
What functions under the
Canada Shipping Act are to be turned over to the commission?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
That is a matter for the
minister to determine from time to time. The commission as set up is advisory to the minister on matters dealt with in the Canada Shipping Act. The minister may or may not turn over executive functions in connection with the act. All such functions are performed by certain departments of government at the moment, whether they will continue to be so performed or whether they will be turned over to the commission to be performed by it, is a matter for the minister to decide.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
Has any decision been
reached as to what functions are to be turned over at the present time?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
There is a strong agitation
for amendments to the Canada Shipping Act. Apparently the act has not been amended for many years. Can the minister say whether

it is the intention to go over it carefully with the idea of bringing it up to date?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Yes. Amendments are being considered. The advice of the commission will be sought in a further examination of the shipping act.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
Is it expected that the act
will be amended at the next session?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Yes, I should think so.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
The second paragraph of
section 8 deals with steamship subventions. What is the policy at the present time with regard to subventions?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
The policy is to maintain
services on certain internal routes in Canada which cannot be self-supporting under the rate structure that the government considers equitable. The needs of the service are examined and the subsidy is fixed at an amount which will permit the service to operate.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
What about shipping
abroad ?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: I know of no present subsidies for external shipping. There does not seem to be any need for any at the moment. The earnings of foreign lines would appear to be ample to permit the companies to carry on without subsidies.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
At the present time the
Department of Trade and Commerce decides what subventions are to be paid, I take it?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Parliament decides the subventions. The Department of Trade and Commerce recommend them. My hon. friend will find in the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce the subventions which are currently being paid.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
Just how is the maritime
commission to fit into that picture? Is it to have the power to recommend subventions direct, or does it merely look into all the facts and then recommend subventions to the minister who, in turn, recommends them to parliament?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
The functions will be administered by the commission. The paragraph reads:
(b) administer, in accordance with regulations of the governor in council, any steamship subventions voted by parliament.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
Does that mean just the
mechanics of paying out subventions, or does it include the power to decide what lines are to get subventions and how large the subventions are to be?

Maritime Commission

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Power to recommend to the minister. Only parliament can vote the money for subsidies. The commission will recommend to the minister, and the minister, if he sees fit, will recommend to parliament the subventions which are required.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
Then there is the third power given in paragraph (c), to:
exercise or perform any other powers, duties or functions conferred on or required to be performed by the commission by or pursuant to any other act or order of the governor in council.
Can the minister give us any indication what type of functions it is proposed to turn over to the commission under that particular paragraph?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: If in a future year the government should pass a bill giving assistance to shipyards, the commission would administer that bill. Likewise, if the government passed a bill subsidizing the construction of steamships, the commission would administer that bill. If any functions now performed by a department of government were turned over to the commission by the minister, the commission would perform those functions.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: The minister pointed out that parliament determined the subventions. I think a wrong meaning might be taken from that. I gather that parliament gives the government power to pay out subventions, but that the government or some agency of the government-in this case the commission -determines what companies may get subventions and what the amount of the subventions may be. I think I am correct in that interpretation, but I am asking for information.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: The minister determines the amount of the subventions that he will recomment to parliament, and the subventions are set out in detail in the estimates. If my hon. friend will look at page 54 of the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, he will find listed there all the subventions to the various companies. Parliament will be asked to vote those subventions.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Then the correct position is this. The exact subvention for a given company appears in the estimates and is passed there, and the government is controlled by that vote. In that event, neither the government nor the commission has power to alter the amount or the rate of subvention as outlined in the estimates. Is that correct?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: I am not in as good a position as I might be to answer that. I see no vote here except specific votes for specific items. There may be a general vote, but I see none in the estimates.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Then in asking for his estimates the minister outlines the companies that are to get this aid, and I suppose at the same time he outlines and tries to satisfy the house as to the rate of assistance to be given.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Then under this legislation you are limited by the amount of the subvention for a given company.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: That is so.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: I just want to get my own ideas on this point clarified. According to section 3(2), this commission is an agent of His Majesty, which, I take it, means an agent of the government, and it can do only such things as the government may refer to it as outlined in this act. If a steamship company should make application for a subsidy or subvention the minister may ask the commission to investigate the matter and make a recommendation as to the subsidy or subvention that would be satisfactory in the circumstances. Then, if the minister agreed with the recommendation he would put an item in the estimates, and it would then be up to parliament?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS UNDER CANADA SHIPPING ACT

speechtext: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply) moved the second reading of Bill No. 340, to establish the dominion coal board.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement on this bill?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I made an extended statement at the time the resolution was intro-

Dominion Coal Board
duced, which I think covers the situation for the moment.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words, because, as we all realize, this is an important bill. I believe the hopes of a great many people in Canada rest upon the success of this board. Much of the discussion during the debate on the resolution was devoted to the question of whether the board should be under one of the departments, or whether it should be independent. As we look back over the history of coal legislation in the dominion, we find that a good many attempts have been made to develop the industry in this country. In 1917, as the minister told us the other day, we had a coal controller. In 1932 we had the dominion fuel board. In 1939 we had a coal administrator. In 1942 we had the emergency coal production board, and now we are trying something else. I understand that this bill has the approval of the operators throughout Canada and also the approval of labour, so that not very much can be said in opposition to the introduction of a measure of this kind. There is provision for seven members on the board, and I suggest that great care should be taken in choosing them. There are five coal producing provinces in Canada, and in fairness to each of those districts or provinces I believe there should be a member from each of them on the board.
As the minister pointed out the other day, no two sections of Canada have the same problems. So far as the maritime provinces are concerned, the problems in Nova Scotia are different from those in New Brunswick. We in New Brunswick have been told that we produce only two per cent of the coal. Nevertheless our coal production is important to us, and I hope that when the board is set up the minister will give consideration to the appointment of a member from New Brunswick.
In the past we have suffered greatly from being linked with Nova Scotia; and I do not say that to the detriment of Nova Scotia, at all. Everyone knows, however, that in Nova Scotia one large company dominates the coal situation. Their interests are entirely different from those of the small operators in New Brunswick; and if only one representative is chosen from the maritime provinces I am satisfied that the difficulties we shall have in the future will be just the same as those we have had in the past. I repeat that when the board is chosen I hope the minister will consider adding a member from New Brunswick.
While the Dominion Coal Company produces about ninety per cent of the coal of Nova Scotia, there are a number of small operators in that province who are in much the same position as we are; and they, of course, should receive consideration.
Another matter that I would bring to the attention of the minister is the wages and employment situation in some parts of the maritimes. We are told there is a surplus of labour; but this condition does not always apply to the mining districts. I know that in the Minto area at the present time there is difficulty in getting men to go into the mines. While there are men without employment in New Brunswick, there are very few available for mining purposes. I understand that some of the operators have applied to have mining labour brought from Europe, but they have been refused1. Mining employment is entirely different from other types of employment, and I hope the board will consider this matter as well as others in connection with coal production.
As I said at the outset, I believe this is a bill which has the general approval of the operators and of labour throughout the Country. I have no serious criticism to make of it, and I sincerely hope it will solve the tremendous problem we have in Canada in connection with coal production.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I. too, shall speak briefly, because I am pleased that an honest-to-goodness effort is now to be made to solve Canada's coal problem. I speak now as a consumer and from the consumer's point of view, as one who uses and has had to use large quantities of coal. Consumers are today harassed to death by the announcements which appear in the press from time to time urging consumers to buy coal, and to buy it now.
In Toronto we stopped using coal for this season no more than two or three weeks ago. I believe it was not until about the 15th of this month that furnaces generally were closed down. In Toronto we burn coal for about nine and a half months of the year, and it is most perplexing to be advised at short intervals through the press to buy coal-buy coal-buy coal-and to be warned constantly of a coal shortage.
There is no reason under heaven why we should have a coal shortage in Canada, if coal production is thoroughly organized, as I now hope it. may be under this measure. During the past few years all of us have been greatly indebted to two of our civil servants who have been working under the direction of the minister in the handling and controlling
Dominion Coal Board

of coal. I refer to Mr. McGregor Stewart of Nova Scotia and Mr. Frank G. Neate of Ottawa. No matter where one goes in Canada, he hears nothing but praise for Mr. Neate. I hope that when the board is set up it will have on it someone like Mr. Neate, who has a thorough knowledge of the coal problems of this country, and that perhaps he may hold one of the principal positions on the board. I would assume that the minister might have in mind the appointment of a lawyer or a judge to act as chairman, of the board, I suggest that if the deputy chairman does not have to be a lawyer, no better man than Mr. Neate could be secured for the job, because he holds the confidence of the public generally.
I hope that when the new board is set up it will have a new plan altogether for approaching this problem. There is plenty of coal in Canada; the problem is to get it to the consumers. For some time past I have been trying to organize a trip up to the Findlay river, one of the two sources of the Peace river. I would hope to go to Fort Grahame, and from there to the Groundhog coal area, as it has been known for many years.
I have no doubt that the department has reports with respect to that area, and the vast deposits of coal said to be located in that basin. The last report I read stated that it had one of the largest, if not indeed the largest coal deposit in the world. I can scarcely believe there is as much coal in that basin as the report I read would seem to indicate. It is pronounced as A-l coal, and it is said that there is none better anywhere. These reports are issued by the department.
If this is so, there can be no reason for a coal shortage in Canada. The Groundhog coal area is located on the upper waters of the Skeena river, and I doubt if it is more than 150 miles, or perhaps less than that, from the mine to Hazelton on the Canadian National. The river is substantial in size, and perhaps if the mines are immediately adjacent to it, through a certain amount of canalization the coal could be brought down to Hazelton and from there in large quantities of probably fifteen or twenty trains at a time, and taken right down to the central provinces.
The city of Toronto with more than 800,000 people should not be in jeopardy at all times for its coal supply. Most people have expensive furnaces or boilers, and they should not have to be uneasy all the time as to whether their installations will be frozen up. Mr. McLURE: Buy it from Alberta.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I believe at present most of the Alberta coal is going to the Pacific 
coast, their closest market. However I was one of the first users in Ontario of Alberta coal at the time the Howard Ferguson government brought down the first shipment of 25,000 tons, and I can say Alberta coal is a splendid fuel. It burns away to an ash, and one has little ash to take out. I used to operate boilers for a week at a time without finding it necessary to remove ashes. I would have given a good deal if I could have had Alberta coal available at all times for use in my house; but we could not get it. I buy oil now, at my home. I am going to suggest to the minister that when this board is set up it be suggested to them that they look into the problem of whether coal from the Groundhog area in northern British Columbia can be brought down to Hazelton and then sent by rail in long train load's to the central provinces.
AVhile I am anything but a socialist, there are some matters that can best be handled like we handle the production of hydro electric power in Ontario. I would be in favour of having this done by the board in order that coal from these deposits may be brought to Ontario. But I certainly advise that they bring down large quantities. The city of Toronto should have a year's supply of coal on hand at all times. This may mean the setting up of large coal dumps along the railroads near to and in the city, but the coal should be there. As I said in the beginning, the people should not be harassed to death over getting coal.
After making an exhaustive survey, I advocated, in one of the early speeches that I made in this house, that a national coal policy be organized. I was not the first to do that, because I believe the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) had done it before. But I doubt if any other member had made a survey of the coal mines from Sydney, Nova Scotia to British Columbia more than I have. If this means a national coal policy, I am all for it. Anything that will give surety to the people of Canada that there will be an ample supply of coal should have the support of all of us.
I am not making any comment at the moment about the setting up of the commission, salaries and so forth, because that will come when the bill is in committee. I hope that a long time coal programme will be laid out to envisage the bringing of maritime as well as western coal to central Canada.
I use maritime coal myself in several boilers, and I know the board of education in Toronto have used many thousand tons of it. It could come up by boat, and there is no reason why it should not. It can be sent up in the summer time so that there will be large supplies

Dominion Coal Board
on hand. In that way the miners in Nova Scotia may be given full-time employment, summer and winter. In the winter time they would be producing what would be shipped by water in the summer.
There is an opportunity to set up a national coal policy which will assure several different things, the first being fair treatment of the men. At different times I have heard the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gilfis) state the conditions under which the miners in Nova Scotia have to w'ork. I believe they must travel several miles from their homes to reach the mines. Speedy transportation should be provided and they should not be crowded into any kind of conveyance.
From my point of view there are not many branches of labour which are more arduous or dangerous than that of coal mining. I think everyone is in favour of these men having, not only fair operating conditions, but proper remuneration, and holidays in which to enjoy the sunlight. They told me when I was in Sydney examining into the coal situation that these men go out three or four miles under the sea. That does not seem just human to me, to expect a man to work without seeing the sunlight and always having his life in jeopardy. No one knows what the bottom of the ocean is like and, while they are under pressure which would prevent a leak, there is always a certain amount of danger. As is stated in the bill, this commission will look into all matters like that.
I hope the commission will organize a programme covering coal mining and the transportation of coal in the speediest way possible from the mines to the consuming public. I know it is a long haul to bring coal to Toronto, say from Hazelton, and it would probably cost $8 to $10 a ton in trainload lots. But we have to have the coal and if our Canadian National Railways is hauling that coal and being paid $8 to $10 a ton for doing so, there will be a smaller deficit to pay at the end of the year. It will be just like taking money out of one pocket and putting it in the other. If the bill will bring about all that the minister has in mind along these lines, I see no reason to oppose it.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the bill was announced I was very hopeful and I still am of what it would bring forth. I realize that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply >(Mr. Howe) can look ahead and see what may happen. I have one or two questions that I should like to ask. Supposing the board recommended to the minister and to the government that there was a national emergency and that 83166-289
the government should take over the coal industry; what would be the action of the government?
We know that in coal mining as in any other industry there are four interested parties. First, there are the people who put up the money; second, there are those who compose management; third, there are the people who do the work, the workers and fourth, there are the consumers. To me the key people are the contented workers. When I went down into a coal mine I was extremely glad to get out alive and still be clean. I have talked to owners of coal mines and they are agreed that, while coal miners receive good wages, they should receive more than any other type of labour because of the daily risks they run and the impairment to their health.
The minister has proved that he knows how to handle workers, and I am sure he will agree that contented coal miners mean a happy management, and that in turn will be remunerative to those who put up the money.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
As the minister knows, in the Crowsnest Pass in British Columbia there are mines to which he made favourable reference in his statement on the resolution. They are mines which throughout the war maintained a very good volume of production in tons per man-day. They kept their equip-
REVISED EDITIO:
Dominion Coal Board

ment modernized and have not had to call on the government throughout the whole war for any production subsidies. In every respect their operations compare most favourably with other coal mines in Canada.
When I was in Fernie and Michel recently I was told about the situation that existed there during the depression. The mines produce good steam coal of an industrial type which is not particularly suited for domestic uses, and seventy-five per cent of their production is taken by the two Canadian Railways. By means of freight subventions they have been enabled to sell their coal as far east as Winnipeg and in such parts of northern Ontario as require rail haul from great lakes ports. One important duty of this board will, I trust, be to see that these favourable mining and operating conditions in Fernie have their beneficial effect in bad times as well as in good, and that the history of the last depression will not be repeated in that part of the country. The Crowsnest Pass towns were much more severely affected by the depression than the general experience in Canada. The people there depend entirely for their existence upon the mines, and I believe that during the depression the mines were closed down entirely for a short period. That was not due, as the minister knows, to the management or the workers, but it was because the market for their coal is a narrow one, confined almost entirely to the railways, and the fact that other industrial markets are quite a distance away. The conditions that prevailed in Fernie in the depression must never be allowed to return,, and I trust that the assurance of markets in bad times as well as in good will be one of the important duties of this board.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I have two questions to ask on this section. One has to do with production. The royal commission on coal pointed out the deplorable production methods in some of the mines in eastern Canada. That is why I have said on different occasions that I did not think it was good policy to subsidize inefficiency. This board will have wide powers and will study and recommend to the minister from time to time such policies as they consider necessary. Will the board have power to go into any mine, whether it is privately-owned or not, and investigate its ability to produce coal efficiently and see whether it is using modern machinery to produce at the cheapest possible cost, which, of course, would be reflected in the wages of the workers? Will the board be able to inspect production also from the point of view of safety regulations?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: The minister said, "any mine that is assisted by subsidy or otherwise." Will the board have power to go into a mine that is not subsidized?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Then on the question of distribution, will this board have the power and will it use that power to ascertain the exact cost of transporting coal from one part of Canada to another? Transportation has been one of the great difficulties in getting markets in eastern Canada, particularly for western coal from Alberta. The transportation costs are tremendous. I remember being on one or two committees of this house where we endeavoured to find the actual transportation costs, but it seemed almost impossible to get that information. One company would give you one figure and another company, another. In view of the fact that transportation subsidies will be given, will this board determine what the actual cost is of transporting a ton of coal, say 100 miles, taking into consideration depreciation and other factors such as the cost of maintaining road bed. I do not believe that information is impossible to obtain, because these are factors which a railway must have taken into account before it fixed its passenger rates, or the cost of hauling western wheat, let us say. The railway must keep accounts so that they can accurately estimate the cost of transporting 100 bushels of wheat a certain distance. The royal commission did not go into that question, and I want to know whether this board will ascertain what transportation costs are, so that it will be in a position to recommend the subsidies that should be given. Such an inquiry would be of great assistance to the western coal mines and the mines in eastern Canada too. Will the board do that job?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
But the question arises, will the board deem it necessary? Members of this house for years past, on every committee that has been set up to look intq the matter, have endeavoured to find out the cost of transporting a ton of coal so-many miles in order that we might determine what subvention was necessary. There has-been a contention, not only among members, but throughout the country, that the railways do not need the amount of subvention they get, that the charge for transporting coal is sufficient to cover the actual cost and give the company a decent profit. Unless there is a definite undertaking by the board, and unless the minister directs the board to do this job, I very much fear that they, like the royal commission, will push this aside and- I use the word advisedly-we may be paying a subvention on an item that is not necessary, so that the government will be losing money in that regard and the people in western Canada and in the maritimes as well will be losing a definite market for their coal.
I now come to the use of coal in Canada. As I said the other day when we were speaking on this question, one of the greatest concerns in Canada at the present time, so far as I can see-and my mind tends naturally toward Alberta, which is a coal-producing area and I live there, though I want to take in the rest of Canada as well-is the necessity for a national fuel policy. Ever since I have been in this house I have tried to emphasize that point, as other members have done as well. We have no monopoly in that regard, but certainly we have emphasized the need of such a policy. In the case of a national emergency such as arose in the last war, I do not think we should be dependent upon other countries for our coal. If we ever get into the situation we were in during the war- and that may easily be-where we have to depend on outside coal for the maintenance of our essential production, it will be a sorry State of affairs for Canada. Coal mining is something that cannot be increased overnight. It does not seem logical to me that a country as rich in coal as Canada is, and with our transportation facilities such as they are, should not be able to transport coal from one end of the dominion to the other on such a basis that it will be sufficient to maintain the productive capacity of our industries. It may be necessary, as I pointed out the other day, that we have a revision of the placement of industries in Canada. I said on more than one occasion during the war that I thought it was the most natural thing for us to establish some of the heavier industries in western Canada where the coal
Dominion Coal Board

supply is at hand and where a share of the raw material for heavier industries is also available within a comparatively few miles, 400 or 500 miles, which does not present a long transportation problem. Labour is such that it can be transported from one province to another with extreme ease. I suggest to the minister, therefore, and to the commission, that if they can find no solution to the transportation problem, so far as coal is concerned, then they should seriously consider the allocation of heavier industries in areas where the coal is situated.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: How can the recommendations of the commission be enforced? What machinery is provided in this act for their enforcement?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: This commission is not a regulatory body in normal times. It is a body to advise the minister on ways and means for the carrying out of the coal policy of the government. In times of emergency it has definite regulatory powers, and an emergency can be proclaimed, whenever the government decides that the situation is getting out of hand.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I understand that this board is to operate in normal times. I do not think it will be feasible to call an emergency situation every time there happens to be a shortage of coal somewhere in Canada. I suggest, therefore, that before the government can formulate and carry out a coal policy which will assure the people of Canada a supply of coal that will be adequate in normal times, the government must have some means of compelling those who produce the coal to carry out the recommendations made by the commission. For instance, there is a scarcity of coal and the board makes certain recommendations to certain coal companies. If the board simiply makes recommendations and the coal companies say, "So what", that does not produce coal. I am wondering what the policy will be for assuring that the recommendations are carried out. I can understand that where a coal mining company is receiving aid from the government the withdrawal of the aid would operate so that the recommendations were carried out, but if the coal company does not see eye;-to-eye with the commission-and remember that the coal company is, after all, operating, not for the welfare of Canada, but for the profit of the shareholders-there is nothing in this act thalt confers any power on the government to assure that the people of , Canada will get the coal which is in Canada.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
The dominion fuel board has been operating for twenty-five years with powers not as extensive as those being granted under this act. In that period, to my know-

ledge it has moved cars of coal from one area to another and from one source to another market and I believe I can say thait there has been no resistance on the part of the owners of the coal to accepting orders from the dominion fuel board. Having had that experience of twenty-five years, I thing it would not be wise for parliament at this time to pass restrictive orders which will probably not be needed. Parliament meets every year; and if we find that additional powers are needed, I presume those powers can be provided.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: The minister said the coal board had been operating for twenty-five years. But has not the coal situation in Canada been pretty much of a mess for twenty-five years?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Well, everybody has been warm.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: If that is all we have to look forward to under this board, it is not too hopeful.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-Powers of the board.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
This afternoon I made a mistake under another bill, when I started to make comments on section 7. At that time I was referring to section 7 of this bill. I did get mixed up. Section 7 embraces a great deal to which the people generally, particularly the consumers, can look with a good deal of hope. For instance, paragraph (a) refers to systems and methods of mining coal. I hope this board will at least have the power to make an investigation itself into the cheapest systems of mining coal and to transmit its findings to the various coal operators. I would not want to think this new board would not be going any farther than the last board went, especially after having listened to the hon. member for Cape Breton South, who is a practical coal man. His observations usually were that in the production of coal in the Nova Scotia mines the machinery and equipment were wholly out of date. If this new board finds that is the case, I would hope it would come forward with some kind of programme to assist in and recommend a faster production of coal in the Nova Scotia mines, or in any other coal mines for that matter; for instance, the mines in the riding of the hon. member for Royal. Last summer I went to one of his towns, namely, Minto, and was amazed to find that they were mining coal in places where the seam was between twenty and thirty inches wide. How a miner can work in that space, I can-

not conceive. Perhaps the board would help to devise some kind of system which would be more effective down there.
Paragraph (c) refers to the development of new uses for coal. If the St. Lawrence canal goes forward, as I hope it will within a reasonable length of time, whatever that length of time is, the development of hydro electric power on the international section, as far as Canada is concerned, will amount to the equivalent of 36,000,000 tons of coal a year; and it will be everlasting. It will be waterpower electricity. Once the St. Lawrence power canal or navigation canal is in operation, it will mean that somebody will have to assist in finding new markets for coal; because if electricity is produced to the equivalent of 36,000,000 tons of coal a year, that is a great deal of coal for which an alternate market will need to be found. The board could do a good service there by-and-by.
Paragraph (e) refers to costs of production and distribution of coal, accounting methods adopted and so on. Right alongside the Peace river west of Hudson Hope-perhaps the minister has been there; I have anyway -is a vast deposit of good coal. During the war I believe his department bought from Gething coal mines the coal that was used all along the Alaska highway. I know that coal mine is right beside the river; the river is down about 250 feet below it. The coal can be shot through chutes from the mines right down to the river. It would go pretty fast down that distance. It can be shot into 500-ton barges. Barges not as large as that but of good size were constructed during the war at Peace River. Peace River barges could be used to take coal down to the town of Peace River on the railway. There would be a vast body of coal for distribution through all northern Alberta south of the Peace river right down as far as Edmonton. I have no doubt that the new board will use its best efforts to bring about the marketing of coal in the various areas in the speediest way possible and, by so doing, cut down the price of coal. The more coal is shipped down, the lower the price.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I am interested in this bill because I have some coal mines in my constituency. I do not consider that the minister was really stating the case correctly when he said that all the people were warm enough in Canada, even though we have had a coal board for the last twenty-five years. Our whole policy in regard to coal should have an overhauling. I notice in section 7 that the terms of reference of the board in regard to research and investigation are quite comprehensive. When the minister
Dominion Coal Board
answers what I have to say, I should1 like him to indicate just what the government would do on the recommendations of such a board.
In my constituency we have had deplorable conditions in the past in the Bienfait mines. Today they are somewhat better, I will admit. But in 1931 when we had the strike there, the redcoats were called in-that is the Royal Canadian Mounted Police-to try to do something about it. We saw the situation of the miners with their low pay and intolerable conditions of work in the mine. When they tried to organize, it did not seem that a solution could be found. That in itself indicated that something should be done.
When we go back to the maritime coal strike which has been going on in the past few weeks, it also indicates that we should have a general overhaul of the coal policy of this country. I should like the minister to indicate, as an example, the policy on what is termed the Kapitu method for the utilization of low grade fuel like we have in my area. We have lignite coal there, which might be used by using the Kapitu method of burning coal underground for the production of power. Would the government undertake, on the recommendation of such a coal board, such policies as they might recommend?
When I was at the Bienfait coal mine about three years ago I found conditions which were intolerable. Prior to the war they were even worse. At that time, when there was a large number of unemployed, the company had stooges among the workers; and if for a moment any workers indicated dissatisfaction with conditions they were quickly let out.
Not only should the people of Canada have an adequate supply of fuel; I believe that we should also protect our workers and that those undertaking the production of coal should be under federal authority. I went into another mine at Estevan. Notwithstanding the fact that certain regulations were on the statute books which, if carried out, would be very good in the way of protecting workers, just prior to my visit a man at the top of the tipple let a couple of coal cars get away from him and roll back down the mine. No one was hurt, simply because no men were coming off work at the time. The regulations require a second entrance for the workers in a mine. In this case there was only the one entrance, and the workers were required to go in and come out of the entrance used for the coal itself. I believe we should have more definite supervision of these mines in order to protect our workers. I do not believe we shall reach a satisfactory solution of our coal problem until we have nationalization of coal.
Dominion Coal Board

In the past we have seen times when our fuel supplies have been low, when people have had to go without. Only a national policy which will take into consideration the need of coal for both industrial and fuel purposes, and under which the government will take responsibility for getting out that coal so that it may be sold to the people at a decent price, will bring about a decent solution of the coal problem of Canada.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I might point out that wages and working conditions in mines, as well as their inspection in connection with safety, are functions of the provinces. I am sorry to see my hon. friend is losing confidence in the government of Saskatchewan.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: When I was at these mines the Liberal government was in'power.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: But I notice that the hon. gentleman is making his remarks today, after the present government has been in for several years.

Section agreed to.
On section 8-Duties of the board.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: These subventions and subsidies are, of course, the very meat of the functions of the board. As I understand it, subventions were first given in order that the coal of Nova Scotia could compete with coal coming from the United States. I want to ask the minister whether subventions are given for the movement of coal within individual provinces. I believe such subventions have been granted in some of the western provinces; but, as far as my own province is concerned, no assistance has been given to the movement of coal within that province, which has made it very difficult for us to compete with coal coming from Nova Scotia. I might point out that a subsidy amounting to $1.67 a ton is paid to the Dominion Coal Company. I understand that they also receive a subvention or assistance in connection with freight rates amounting to $3.47 a ton, making a total of $5.14 a ton given Nova Scotia coal by way of assistance. That was paid on the coal moved into New Brunswick. Coal produced in New Brunswick received a subsidy of only $1, so that there was a difference of $4.14. This matter was continually brought to the attention of Mr. Brunning, who was head of the board during the war, but nothing was done.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: All the coal found a market, did it not?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Yes, all the coal found a market.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Then your complaint is that the operators did not make enough money?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: My complaint is that the operators of New Brunswick are carrying on at a loss, whereas coal coming from Nova Scotia received this large amount of help. I am not objecting to Nova Scotia getting this help, but I say assistance should be given New Brunswick for the movement of coal within that province. I believe it is shown in the report of the Carroll commission that assistance was given to British Columbia, for example, in connection with the movement of coal from the mines to certain sections of that province. I make a special plea for the coal mines in New Brunswick, because that is my own province. I am interested in general in the production of coal throughout the dominion, but I know the operators of my province have suffered during the last number of years because of the policies of this government, and they received very little sympathy from Mr. E. J. Brunning, who was administering our coal operations during the war. That is one reason why I have particularly asked the minister, when this board of seven men is set up, to see that consideration is given to appointing a man from New Brunswick. Our coal area is small, and in the past I have understood that for this reason no sympathy has been given, or at least not as much sympathy as should have been given. We were simply brushed aside and told, "You have only two per cent of the coal, so it does not make very much difference." That is why I am calling this matter to the attention of the minister. I do not say the minister himself has been unsympathetic, but he has been a very busy man. These matters have been looked after by other people, and New Brunswick has not received the attention to which it is entitled. They have almost ruined the coal industry in that province.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: That is a very serious charge. The earnings of every coal operator in New Brunswick are a matter of record with the emergency coal production board. I can give my hon. friend the list of operators and the profits they made, if he wishes. But I can testify to this, that during the period of the emergency coal production board no operator in New Brunswick went bankrupt.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I am not saying that. Is it necessary for a man to go bankrupt before the government will step in and give the assistance that is being given other people? I did not say these men went bankrupt; I said the industry as a whole lost money. Not only

Dominion Coal Board
that, but these men came to Ottawa at different times and made representations, and they received scant consideration.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: It is a serious thing for a member to stand up in the House of Commons and say the industry in New Brunswick lost money during the war. On what does he base that statement?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: On the facts.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
