subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I will carry my charge before any committee; and I can take the Carroll report and show where these men lost money. If the minister has read this report through he must have seen that. I am not saying they all lost money.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: You said the industry lost money.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I said the industry in general lost money.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: It is all very well for a member to stand up in the house and abuse a board that carried heavy responsibilities during the war, mentioning the chairman by name and saying he was unfair and discriminatory. I think a little careful consideration is required before an hon. member takes action in that manner.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I thank the minister very much for telling me what I should and should not do.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I would expect you to know.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I have heard the chairmen of boards criticized in this house, and I offer no apology for criticizing the chairman of this board.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Very poor taste.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I have had representations from the miners of my province and my constituency, and they have not been at all backward about criticizing the chairman of this board. I have not the least doubt they have criticized him to the minister as well.

Section agreed to.
Sections 9 and. 10 agreed to.
On section 11-Regulating and controlling production, distribution and use of coal.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I pointed out, in introducing the resolution, that it seemed to me that parliament should' consider an extension of the
emergency powers. We are taking that emergency power in respect of coal, for the reason that the coal situation is not within the jurisdiction of Canada by itself. A large proportion of the coal Canada uses must be imported from outside this country.
The same applies to fuel oil. Therefore I suggest an amendment to the section which would give the government the same emergency powers in the matter of fuel oil that it is taking in the matter of coal. In other words, if a situation should arise where suffering would result because of Canada's not obtaining sufficient fuel oil, or because of an improper distribution of fuel oil, emergency powers could be invoked under the bill as they can be in respect of coal. Therefore I would ask my colleague to move an amendment on this point.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I move:
That section ,H be amended by-
(a) changing the word "coal" wherever it appears in section il'l to the word "fuel," and
([b) adding as sub-section (7) the following:
(7) "Fuel" includes coal, light and heavy fuel oil including bunker "C" fuel oil, kerosene, range oil, gas oil. diesel oil and any other hydrocarbon fuel used for the same purposes as the above-designated grades.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Would the minister explain how that changes the bill? I am thinking particularly of British Columbia where much of our fuel is wood and. sawdust. I suggest that some care should be given before the government takes in all fuels from one end of Canada to the other. I have no doubt that the minister was thinking particularly of oil; but when he uses the word "fuel" he brings in wood. And I am. not so sure; that wood and sawdust should be brought in.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: There is no intention to apply the emergency provision to wood. The only intention is to include coal and liquid fuel oil.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Is natural gas included in the list of hydro-carbons?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: No, it is not.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
It will be noted that section 11
(1)	states:
Where the governor in council is of opinion that by reason of conditions or events within or outside of Canada there is or is likely to be a shortage of coal in Canada of such dimensions or nature as to imperil the welfare or national life of Canada . . .
Action may be taken to conserve the available supply of coal and to regulate and control its production, distribution and use. In my opinion there are two types of emergency which may face our coal industry. As one
Dominion Coal Board

who represents a constituency in which a considerable amount of Coal mining is conducted, I feel concerned about the second type, and that is a condition which may develop under which we find our miners are out of employment and our mines are permitted to close down or to slow down production, actions which in themselves may result in a condition which this bill is designed to meet, should such condition arise.
I should like to see the board given authority to give just as much consideration to a national emergency of the kind to which I have referred as to an emergency where an actual shortage of coal production occurs. Under this bill, should stagnation within the industry develop, I suggest that the board should then proceed to take whatever action is necessary to maintain the industry in a sound and flourishing position. Would the minister indicate whether, as part of its work, the board may give attention to that aspect of a national emergency?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
The sole purpose of the bill is to set up a board which will keep the coal industry in a healthy condition. It is the duty of the commissioners to carry out that mandate. The emergency arises when a situation develops which the commission, under its ordinary duties and authorities, cannot handle, a situation which imperils the welfare of the nation. I think my hon. friend would hardly look to the emergency section to take care of the problem he mentions.
Mr. S'HAW: It has always been my opinion that it is far better to head off an emergency by taking appropriate action than to try to meet it once it has come. Once again I urge that, in turn, the board be urged to do everything possible Iby every conceivable type of action to try to prevent our rushing headlong into an acute emergency involving a coal shortage.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I was about to speak along the same lines as the hon. member for Red Deer. Would the minister indicate whether or not we are now facing a real shortage of fuel oil, and that next winter we shall be finding ourselves short of it. People who have been contemplating the installation of oil furnaces are now told not to instal them. Then, the authority of the board should be wide enough to see to it that all possible coal is mined between now and next fall to produce every bit of coal we can. Would the minister indicate that, provided that a coal strike should come, or that some mines should shut down for
one reason or another, the board would have authority to open those mines to see that coal is produced?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: It will be the duty of the board to make sure there is sufficient fuel in the country to protect the life of the country. The fact that a man would like to put in an oil burner and cannot be guaranteed a supply of fuel oil for that purpose scarcely constitutes a national emergency. But if there were any section of the country which did not have fuel of any kind, that might be a national emergency. The board would act in the matter of liquid fuel only if a situation of that kind developed; that is, if the lack of oil fuel became so serious that the national interests were prejudiced.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Section 11 states that the governor in council may be of the opinion that a shortage of fuel exists, and that it may declare a national emergency. The governor in council would be a comparatively small number of men. How could they override the rights of the provinces; because it is the provinces which have the control of their own natural resources?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
The wording of the bill was taken from the latest ruling of the privy council in England, when consideration was had as to what constitutes a national emergency which enables the federal government to take over jurisdiction. The hon. member is right when he states that the operation of coal mines is a provincial matter, unless a situation arises which is described under this bill as an emergency. In such circumstances the privy council has ruled that the right to act passes to the federal government.
Mr. JOHlNSTON: Would; it not be better to have it the governor in council in consultation with the provinces? It seems to me that that would be a more amicable arrangement than to just have the governor in council declare an emergency.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I suppose it would use common sense. This idea of consulting with the provinces is not unheard of, as I think my hon. friend will admit. The wording is this:
Where the governor in council is of opinion that by reason of conditions or events within or outside of Canada there is or is likely to be a shortage of coal in Canada of such dimensions or nature as to imperil the welfare or national life of Canada as a whole ....
That is a pretty serious situation and, when that happens, the federal government takes such action as it considers adequate. It does not need much advice as to what it does.

Dominion Coal Board

speechtext: I am not just clear as to what .the minister means. I take it he has indicated that the purpose of his amendment was to bring fuel oil under the jurisdiction of this board?

speechtext: No.

speechtext: While we were in the resolution stage, I asked the minister to tell us what would be the extra cost of setting up this board over and1 above the cost of the government supervision of the coal industry as it has been exercised in the past.

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OF ROCKY MOUNTAINS-AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA

speechtext:
Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Acting Minister of Mines and Resources) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to approve a certain agreement between the dominion of Canada and the government of Alberta respecting the protection and conservation of the forests on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains and to provide for the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of sums required for capital expenditures, payments to the province of moneys for formulated programmes carried out by the province, salaries of officers and employees appointed under the act and expenses incidental to the operation of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OF ROCKY MOUNTAINS-AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA
speechtext:
This bill proposes to ratify an agreement which has been, entered into between the government of the province of Alberta and His Majesty the King, represented by the Department of Mines and Resources, to provide for certain expenditures in protecting the east slope of the Rocky mountains. Hon. members are aware that the east slope of the Rocky mountains is the locality of the head waters of two great rivers of Canada, the Saskatchewan and the Athabaska. Both the North Saskatchewan and the South Saskatchewan rivers and their tributaries are dependent largely upon the run-off from the east slope of the Rocky mountains for the maintenance of water levels throughout the year.
The east slope of the Rocky mountains was transferred to the province of Alberta with the transfer of natural resources. The interests involved in protecting, the east slope of the Rockies are not confined to one province. The work is of equal importance to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba and. Alberta. The government of Alberta have made representations to the federal government that that province is unable to finance the expenditures required to carry out the protection that all interested parties agree is required. The agreement provides that certain federal assistance will be given in carrying out a five-year programme for the purpose of clearing up a situation on the east slope that is harmful to the water resources of that area. Thus the agreement makes provision for a division of the responsibility between the federal government and the government of Alberta.
May I suggest that extensive discussion of this measure might, be reserved until the bill and the agreement are before us. The bill itself is very simple. The agreement is more complicated, and we can discuss both intelligently when we have the bill and the agreement before us.

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OF ROCKY MOUNTAINS-AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA
speechtext:
I personally take a certain amount of humble satisfaction out of this resolution because, as the minister knows, for some years, after much travel on the east slope of the Rockies, I have been advocating just such a bill. The time has long, since passed when the federal government should come forward and assist the Alberta government to protect the east slope of the Rocky mountains so far as financing goes, because this is not purely an Alberta question. The reclamation and maintenance of the forests on the east slope of the Rocky mountains affect the whole watershed, particularly of the Saskatchewan river, not so much of the Athabaska river because the latter river flows off to the northeast, but the maintenance of the forests on the east slope of the Rocky mountains does affect the watershed of the Saskatchewan river very much, both north and south, particularly west of the Alberta, border. That comprises 125,000 square miles, which is a large area. West of the Alberta border the watershed of the North Saskatchewan is about
50,000	square miles, and the watershed of the South Saskatchewan is about 66,000 square miles. For years past those forests have been badly denuded and destroyed, principally by fire. I calculated a few days ago from data that, I have, and which of course, the government has, that I would be putting it midly if I said that an average of 20,000 acres have been destroyed by fire each year on the eastern slope. At the head waters of the Brazeau and of the Red Deer and of the branches of the South Saskatchewan, it is sad to see whole areas on which the forests have been destroyed by fire. So that the government is to be commended on this agreement with the province of Alberta to prevent forest fires by

Forest Conservation
the regular means by which such fires are prevented.
I hope that when the minister again speaks he will tell us what the programme of protection is. If it is stated in the bill he does not need to take time to tell us now. There should be a long-range programme covering the number of acres or square miles that are to be protected and replanted each year and the methods by which the water is to be piped through the foothills and the eastern slope for the protection of the forests.
I found when I was in conference last October with the officials of the United States bureau of reclamation in Denver, Colorado, that they have a substantial programme for forest protection and the prevention of fires on the east slope of their Rocky mountains. They count it as an important part of their programme of reclamation, and so it is, because in that area, principally in the centre of their east slopes, the river basin is much like our own Saskatchewan river basin. So much depends upon the preservation of the forests, not only water for agriculture which will be required when our departments bring to completion the proposed reclamation of the dried-out areas through irrigation, but water for domestic purposes in the cities and towns that we hope to see grow on the banks of the Saskatchewan river when that whole area is reclaimed; also it is important for power production and for the conservation of wild life. The United States bureau of reclamation in Denver attach a lot of value to their wild life. They have many pictures illustrating the disasters which have overtaken their forest animals through fire, and I have no doubt that on our eastern slope of the Rocky mountains fire has caused great destruction to our wild life.
So it is an important programme. I have a recollection that the Minister of Mines and Resources either stated in the house or told me personally that the amount to be contributed to the Alberta government runs into three or four millions-[DOT]

speechtext:
Before this section carries, I should like to point out to the committee that this and the other clauses in the bill were referred after second reading to the standing committee on external affairs. While there, this clause received careful scrutiny by members, with the result that in the subsequent clause one finds the single amendment which the committee finally approved and submitted by way of recommendation to the committee of the whole house.
On this particular clause, without attempting to make any further observations, since I think we have already discussed practically all the matters of prime importance touching the principle of the bill, and perhaps its details as well, I wonder if the minister is in a position to tell us whether or not there are any countries other than those which he mentioned in his original speech on the second reading, which have since completed their procedure along lines similar to those we are now following. In other words, what other countries have delegated their authority from their legislature to their executive as is proposed in this bill?
Another question I would raise at the moment is the one that arises from the discussions which took place in the committee itself. It seems that- there are two different ways by which the executive may be clothed with authority by the legislative branch in a matter such as this. In the earlier days, under the old league of nations, the clothing of the executive with powers from the legislative body came, I understand, through a blanket statute or authority passed at the time when the league covenants were before the house. An entirely different procedure is envisaged in this legislation, and perhaps will be envisaged in others, namely, that piece by piece, apparently, the government intends to ask for the clothing of that authority by the legislative body; and one of the external affairs officials indicated that he thought that was a

sensible way of handling the matter. But the minister was not there, and for that reason we were not able to receive definite answers as to policy, which only the minister at this stage of the proceedings can properly give us.
I would be glad if he would comment on the reasons. I am not raising any criticisms with respect to them, but I think we should have some clarification, because in the days that lie ahead we may be asked to deal with other bills arising out of our commitments and obligations under the united nations charter, and the position should be made clear to the committee at this time. Perhaps the minister will give us some explanation.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: With respect to the first question, as to what other countries have clothed the executive branch of their sovereignty with powers required to carry out the directives that may be made by the security council, the former inquiry had to do with the British commonwealth countries, and I mentioned some.- I am not sure whether I mentioned at that time the action that had been taken by the legislative assembly at New Delhi. We did get information that there had been introduced and passed by the legislative assembly at New Delhi a bill much in the form of this and of the legislation adopted by other British commonwealth units, empowering the governor to make orders, which would become effective upon publication in their official gazette, to carry out such directives as might properly be made by the security council under article 41 of the charter.

speechtext:

speechtext:

Mr. ST. LAURENT: No. I do not think the question has been looked upon as urgent in view of the fact that the security council has not yet put itself in a position where it would be able immediately to make directions under this article 41 of the charter, even if any such should be considered as desirable.
To answer the second question, the covenant of the league of nations was ratified by

United Nations
Canada in the form of a statute. Legislation was passed which made the covenant a part of the law of Canada and empowered the governor in council to take such action as might be required in order to comply with the obligations undertaken by accepting the covenant. Hon. members will recall that the form of the ratification of the charter of the united nations which was suggested and passed, was resolutions of both houses of parliament requesting His Majesty to ratify in the name of Canada. That did not constitute legislation. The real reason for coming from time to time only with such things as the government is prepared to recommend to parliament is the anxiety which was expressed many times in this house over the giving of blanket authority to the executive branch of the state. There are occasions when it may be necessary, in the interests of the security of the state, to get blanket authority; but this did not appear to be a case where it could be seriously stated that there would be apt to be danger to the security of the state without blanket authority. Under those conditions it was felt that it would be complying better with the temper of this house to ask only for the things which appeared to be necessary and not to take for the executive branch any greater powers than the House of Commons would feel it was reasonable to grant.

subtopic: POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41
speechtext:
I think the government will keep out of trouble better that way than by following some other suggestions.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It was felt that in that way the immediate interests of the country would be safeguarded and we would not be asking the House of Commons to commit itself to anything which is not foreseen at this time. Therefore it was felt that it would be better, even at the risk of having to come back more than once, to have a real case every time some transfer of authority from parliament to the executive branch of the government was being sought. When I was speaking
about Ripple Rock just before the committee rose the other day, the minister interjected to ask me if I had a written statement from Colonel Swan as to his opinion on the offer of the Malahat Shipping Company. I have no statement from Colonel Swan, but I have a newspaper clipping from the Vancouver Sun of March 27 last in which Colonel Swan is quoted as being in general approval of the method advanced by Captain Lawson. One short part of this article reads:
One of these schemes which I examined is that of Captain Lawson of this city, and a second by B. F. Lundy, also of Vancouver. I feel certain there is certainty that such a method would be successful.
That is my authority for the statement I made the other night. I have on my file a list of various organizations in Vancouver which have stated they are in favour of this plan. Without taking up more time of the committee, I think this is a good place for me to make my point to the minister. Here is a rock which it would be very advisable to remove. The department has attempted to remove it on previous occasions, and there is a considerable public demand in British Columbia for its demolition. This company comes along and puts up a proposition for the removal of the rock on a no cure, no pay basis. The minister's department very properly enunciated three prerequisites to a contract. Those conditions are that the minister is satisfied with the technical assistants, that the company has adequate financial backing, and that No. 2 rock will be removed. Surely a year after the original offer was made this matter could be settled one way or the other, not by my saying whether or not I have Colonel Swan's signed affidavit, but by the minister's department getting in touch with Colonel Swan, the engineer upon whom
Captain Lawson apparently relies. If what Captain Lawson says proves to be the case, you can go ahead. If it proves not to be the case, you can turn the offer down. But it seems to me that a matter like this cannot be settled from a distance of 3,000 miles. Surely there is enough here to warrant the minister going into it thoroughly and accepting the offer if it is good or rejecting it if it is bad. I see no reason why this matter should go on month by month in an indeterminate state. That is the particular point I wish to bring to the minister's attention now. He said that there had been thirteen different suggestions since the last work was done on the rock. I feel that all those thirteen suggestions should be taken seriously and a decision made on each of them. I think that on the particular proposition I have mentioned to the committee there is enough to warrant investigation and to require a decision to be made.

speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
I should like the hon. member to understand that there is no finality concerning a project of this kind. We have tried for years to remove the rock and we have spent large sums of money, but the time came when even those wTho had made favourable reports, just as Mr. Swan believed that such a scheme would succeed, had to admit that no headway was being made. On the other hand, every day that went by, the costs were piling up on the government and we could not see the end of the project even with the best methods that my engineers thought could be applied. That involved a barge being held by overhead cables. The government at one time decided to dispose of the barge, pay the accounts, and instruct our engineers to study other means that might be suggested or that could be devised. Even at that time I sent my chief engineer, Mr. Cameron, one of the outstanding engineers in the country, who has since retired, out there. That was the last work he did in the department. He spent three weeks out on the coast in the fall of 1945 and a few months afterwards resigned or was superannuated. I have to rely on my own engineers for their judgment on the different schemes suggested. The last scheme that Mr. Lawson suggested was a kind of platform which would be held by cables, as we try to hold the barge, but still my engineers say that you cannot proceed with drilling from a platform which is held only by cables. There has to be some way of stabilizing that platform by some anchor-
Supply -Public Works

age. I do not think there are many engineers who could agree on a practical method of blasting that rock.
The hon. member says that we should not delay month after month and year after year. I am not so sure but that prudence would caution us to be very careful, because during three or four years we have continued to spend the people's money and to get no results. The last estimate we received was for nearly $2 million. If we made that expenditure and got no results, would I receive the approval of members of parliament for making that expenditure? Members could easily find some reason for saying:	You
should not have gone ahead so quickly about this but should have got more advice. My own engineers are doubtful about it, but there are so many people who are not engineers who think they know how it should be done. Opinions come from everybody. When I was out there I did not know what to do to get away from all the telephone calls I was receiving. I would inquire if they were engineers, and they would say no, but that they knew how to blast this rock out of Seymour Narrows.
Before I would recommend to the government that an appropriation be placed in the estimates to proceed with this work, I would need more advice than we have received. I must say that I was not impressed with the last letter the company wrote to us with respect to the "no cure, no pay" offer. We had inquired into the financial standing of that company and whether they had experienced personnel, and they took a very long time to reply. I have not read one of the last letters. They still maintain the "no cure, no pay" proposition, but they have started to say: You could make some advance to us when we start on the work. That is not a "no cure, no pay" proposition, if we are to make progress payments.
That is not my information. In the letters I have had there is no suggestion of anything but the "no cure, no pay" basis.

I have not read the letter myself. I am taking the word of my deputy minister, and I am sorry I said that if it was not a fact because I would not want to harm the case of these gentlemen. When we asked them whom they had employed for engineering advice they mentioned Mr. Swan. I am advised that, though he thinks this method would be a good one, he is not ready to go as bondsman to guarantee the completion of the work by that scheme. I am putting it fairly to the hon.

member. If he had the responsibility of the expenditure of the money and his officers, the engineers of his department, were not satisfied that the scheme would succeed, I do not know what position he would take. But personally I am hesitant about it.
Does the minister say that his engineers have gone into this specific proposition of the Malahat Shipping Company and made all the inquiries they consider necessary about it?
Perhaps they can go farther in their study of the conditions, but the report I received was that the platform scheme is only a modification of the barge scheme held in place by overhead cables.

I do not want to get into a discussion of engineering details, but I understand that the platform will not be held in place by overhead cables but will be set in the rock. I am only asking now that the minister take this offer seriously and see to it that the appropriate officers of his department investigate it thoroughly both from the engineering side and as to the financial backing of the company. If he finds either that they have not a proper system or have not the requisite finances behind them, then I shall not be heard from any more. But I do not like the matter left in this uncertain state where, so far as I can find out, everything has been done by correspondence and there has been no move by the department to go to Vancouver and look into Captain Lawson's offer thoroughly. I suggest that that be done.

This rock happens to be in my riding and I think I should have a few words to say about it. The hon. member for Vancouver Burrard has brought up a subject that merits a hearing, and if this is truly a "no-cure, no pay" proposition I can see no reason why the minister would not consider it seriously. I myself would think that probably a fair proposal would be to say to them: You start it. After all, I can assure you that no one can do any harm to that rock, and if they knocked ten feet off it would be fair to pay them one-third of the cost, and if they knocked twenty feet off, pay them another third. As far as engineering ability is concerned, that is something I would not emphasize too much. In my opinion we had too much engineering ability on it the last time. The removal of Ripple rock is not an ordinary engineering problem. I think a number of hard-rock miners and good loggers would do a good job on it. As

Supply-Public Works
regards the menagerie that existed there the last time, I had difficulty in explaining to the people of Campbell River and the adjacent area how it was that the government could find money to spend up there and still could not provide funds for necessary public works. I think we should know definitely whether this is a "no-cure, no pay" proposition. I would not be afraid of that rock. They cannot do it any harm, and if they blasted ten feet off into the water they would have proved that they had a sound proposition. I would not stop them from going ahead to that extent. Probably it is not the way in which a government does things, but I could never understand why it would not call for tenders.
We did.
Have you ever called for tenders?
The first time we asked for tenders we received a firm price of $250,000, and * they did not even put the barge in place with that amount.
You did not pay the money in that case?
Yes. Actually we have paid $892,000, and when people ask me for floats and breakwaters along the coast when I have spent some $900,000 I feel sore.
You should feel ashamed.

Last year I congratulated the minister on stopping the work that was being carried on there because I thought he had done a wise thing, and before he starts again I would suggest that he get a firm tender without any money in advance until he gets some rock blown off.

The other night mention was made of some of the offices owned by the department. I believe the city council of Ottawa a few months ago discussed the smoke nuisance. I do not think it is much use trying to clean up the offices until such time as the government stops the smoke nuisance, because I have noticed from the parliamentary restaurant here, looking down at the temporary building, that during cold weather the stack throws off smoke for an hour at a time and that smoke drifts over to the supreme court building and over the city. Look over to the union station and you will see the stack behind that station throwing off smoke hour after hour, though only on certain days. Look at the national revenue building; at certain times-not at all times but sometimes- the stack there throws off smoke that blankets
the Chateau Laurier hotel. That is why I believe their curtains have to be washed so often. The curtains in my room get black in about two weeks' time. I was wondering whether there was some way the department could check on that. A year ago I mentioned the Daly building, and since that time the stack there has not thrown off smoke. The engineers must have done a good job on the oil furnaces. I suggest that the other furnaces need checking on. The minister should get after them and see if something cannot be done.
We did do something at the Daly building.
Yes, and that is clean now.
Down here we have the central heating plant for all these buildings and they are lower down. We will take a note of what the hon. gentleman has said.

There must be some way of stepping the excessive smoke. It happens only at certain times, but when it comes it blankets all that part of the city and the supreme court building. There is another building I am thinking of. I do not know whether it belongs to the Department of National Revenue or is in the income tax section, but the stack there throws off smoke in clouds, and the prevailing wind is from that direction to the Chateau Laurier. It certainly covers everything, and I believe we get some of that smoke in the House of Commons.
Also the sulphur.
Yes, but that is not a government project. Can the minister tell me whether the government owns all eight buildings that are occupied by the national film board, or whether some of these are rented?
Most of them are rented. They occupy, I believe, four or five.
I believe there are eight buildings altogether.
There are eight. We own the John street building and we put up a fireproof building for storing films. They have space on Sparks street.
Which is expensive space.

It is all quite expensive, but the film board has eight different locations and the situation is far from being satisfactory. That is why there was a certain vote to prepare plans.

Can they not go into one of these temporary buildings built during the war?

They are all occupied. All the buildings here, except space at the records building on the farm and except for changes that are being made every once in a while in the city, are occupied. As I told the committee the other night, we own fifty-two buildings in Ottawa and rent ninety-six. Though the space situation is not as bad as it was eighteen months ago, it is still not satisfactory.
What is the rental?
Perhaps the hon. gentleman will let me proceed. I am on the general item now and I will give the information as soon as we reach his question.
There was something else that struck me last winter. When we had a heavy fall of snow I noticed that the trucks were running down here-
That does not come under my department but under the federal district commission.
I wish to direct a question to the minister regarding the proposed federal building for Flin Flon, Manitoba. The minister has had many communications-[DOT]
For three hours we have been discussing general questions. When we get to the architectural branch in that province I will answer the question with regard to Flin Flon.

speechtext: Will you accept the question even if there is not a vote?
Certainly. Any building you wish to suggest.

With reference to Ripple Rock, I wish to take this opportunity of thanking the minister for the work which is being done in Nanaimo harbour where he has done a great deal of dredging and is improving the vharf there. I should not like him to think that is the only work which is necessary around the coastline of Vancouver island. I could name quite a number of other places which need not only fishermen's floats, but wharves, breakwaters and dredging, in exactly the same way as the hon. member for Halifax went around his coastline and mentioned every fishing village there. If any money is to be saved by discontinuing the work on the blowing up of Ripple Rock-which my fishermen consider in the main a menace to the Yankee skippers who do not know those waters; my fishermen

can go over it at any time-I should like it to be spent in the constituency of Nanaimo. I have not a great deal of hope because there is no by-election coming along this year, but I still live in hope.

speechtext:
Once again I should like to ask the minister a question with respect to wages and holidays with pay for cleaning women in public buildings. This is a matter which I have discussed with the minister before on a number of occasions. I appreciate the fact that he has given attention to it and from time to time has been able to have certain improvements made. In fact, this very year an improvement was made with respect to holidays and sick leave for these women. Prior to this year, there was no general provision for holidays or sick leave, but owing to the requirements of the provincial law in Manitoba arrangements were made two or three years ago for the women there to get six days' holiday or sick leave a year, but the one exhausted the other. However, this year the minister changed that and made it a general provision throughout the service so far as this work is concerned. The women now get six days' holidays with pay a year; and in addition to that, they are entitled, if they are off sick, to six more days without loss of pay. I can assure the minister that this provision is very much appreciated. However, so far as the women working in the public buildings of Winnipeg are concerned, I would point out that this announcement was not of as much an advantage to them as it was to the women here in Ottawa, because they already had the six days' holidays a year with pay. I would point out to the minister that the hours of work there are a little longer than they are here. The reason is obvious. For example, in this building the women must do the work in the morning; but in Winnipeg the work is done in the evening and it is possible for them to work for a longer period of time. Many of these women are getting along in years. Many are widows who have been forced to find work of this kind in order to keep themselves going. I am sure the minister will agree with me that it is not too much to suggest that they should have two weeks' holidays a year. I hope he will continue the good work he has done in interesting himself in the case of these women, and will try to get that extension at as early a day as possible.
Just before the minister made his announcement about these improvements on February

Supply-Public Works
6 of this year, there was some press publicity with regard to what was coming. Unfortunately, the publicity went a little farther than the minister's statement went, because it indicated that, in addition to the holidays and sick leave to which I have referred, there would be some increases in pay. The minister's statement did not include that. When I questioned him about it, he told me that the matter of recommending rates of pay for these women comes under the Department of Labour. Subsequently I directed my questions to the Minister of Labour with regard to this matter, and on February 10 he made a reply which reads in part as follows, as reported at page 252 of Hansard:
The Department of Labour has undertaken a survey to ascertain whether on the basis of prevailing rates of pay this particular group of employees is entitled to an increase in remuneration.
I allowed a considerable period of time to elapse, until April 29, when I again directed a question to the Minister of Labour as to whether that survey had been completed. In his reply on that date, as recorded at page 2518 of Hansard, the minister said:
Since the beginning of the year the Department of Labour, on the request of the departments concerned, has made recommendations with respect to wage rates for this class of service at the following points: Toronto, Hamilton, Windsor, London, Winnipeg, Montreal, Kingston. Brantford, Kitchener. Vancouver, Sudbury, Wallaceburg and Saint John, New Brunswick.
That statement of the minister suggests that recommendations with respect to wage rates had been made at those various points, but does not say whether any changes in wage rates had been made. The present minister's statement, as he will recall, did not cover wage rates. It just covered holidays with pay and sick leave. The concluding sentence in this same reply of the Minister of Labour was as follows:
The survey to which my hon. friend refers, and which I mentioned on February 10, is not yet completed.
So far as the rumoured increases in wages for these women are concerned, that means that nothing had happened up until April 29. At that point it seems that the Minister of Public Works was still waiting for the Minister of Labour to have his survey completed and make a recommendation to him. I recognize that there has to be this reference from one department to another in the government service and that there has to be a proper allocation of jurisdiction. I also recognize that the Minister of Public Works has shown an interest in these women, and I know he will do everything he can to expedite the
matter in the proper way. So I am asking him now if he can tell the committee whether anything has happened since April 29, and in particular if he will continue to do his best on these two counts: (1) the matter of extending to two weeks the holidays with pay, particularly for those who work longer hours, as is the case in Winnipeg; and (2) the matter of continuing his negotiations with the Department of Labour looking toward an increase in pay for these women cleaners.
To answer the first question, the difficulty is that these are part-time employees who work two or three hours a day.
For how many months a year?

They work the year round. But actually, since February, the government has granted six days' or a week's holidays with pay and six days' sick leave. Now the request is for two weeks' holidays with pay. That would come in line with the ordinary civil servant. We compare what we do in the service with what is done in industry elsewhere. The objection is that in Ottawa they work for only two or two and a half hours in the morning; they do not work all day. If they were working all day I am told two weeks' holidays would be quite justified, but in view of the few hours of work they do a day it would be hardly justifiable to give them two weeks' holidays. My officials give me examples from other cities in the country where people are employed part time, and where they are given only one week's holidays with pay. That does not mean I agree with that policy. I live in this district and have been living here for a long time. I know a great many of the 'people working in this district; I sympathize with their case, and I think I have been their advocate for a good many years.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is right.

I am still very well disposed toward them, but I am not the only one who has to decide these matters. One thing is certain: I do not offer any opposition when a good suggestion comes to the fore.
As to the second point, in connection with salaries, in every town and city mentioned by the Minister of Labour inquiries were made and increases were given in the rates of pay. There are none of those places where there w-ere not increases following the investigation. Perhaps my hon. friend does not exactly understand the procedure that must be gone through. Public works, who employ and pay
Supply-Public Works

these people, get a request from Toronto, for instance, saying, here are the conditions of work, and the salary does not equal that paid by other industries in the same locality. We send a request to treasury board, which advises us in this matter, and treasury board goes to the labour department, which carries on the survey and makes a report. Then, when treasury board makes a decision it is confirmed by the cabinet. Public works does not interfere at all in the fixing of these rates, except to make representations to treasury board that for similar work outside or in other departments the rates are not similar. We await a recommendation from the labour department to treasury board. I think we are paying the rates paid in the locality by others employing the same kind of labour.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I appreciate the comment of the minister, and if my previous remarks are checked over I think it will be noted that I referred to the difference between the hours of work here in Ottawa and the hours of work in Winnipeg, where I am a little more familiar with the situation. I know that in this very building for example, the women come in the morning and work for a very short period of time. In the dominion public building and the customs building in Winnipeg, for example, they work in the evening. I would rather not state the time, because I dislike making any statement that is not exact, but I believe their working time runs to about six hours a night. I know the total number of hours they work a week comes so close to the hours listed in the Manitoba provincial law that the minister recognized a few years ago that they should be treated as full-time employees in that province. I do not like to make a distinction between the women in one city and those in another. The minister would agree with me, I know, that the best that possibly can be done for them all across the country should be done. But I ask him to consider, and to have his officials consider, that women who are working, let us say six hours a day, putting in thirty-six or thirty-eight hours a week, or maybe more -because they work six nights a week in Winnipeg-are in a little different position with respect to this matter of two weeks' holidays a year.
I shall have my officials look into that case.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

I (rust that will be done from the angle I have indicated, because I point out to the minister it was that difference what buildings we rent for the use of this film years ago to provide one week's holidays with

pay for these people in cities like Winnipeg, even before it was done here.

I mention that date, because at that time the Minister of Labour said the survey to which I have referred, and which he had mentioned on February 10, had not been completed.

No. These investigations and surveys in regard to rates of pay go on the year round. I think I signed' something not long ago making a recommendation to the treasury board for an increase in regard to London or some other city. This process goes on all the time. Under this item provision is made for ninety-five elevator operators. Can the minister tell us if any of these men are on the permanent staff?
We have ninety-six permanent elevator operators and 156 temporaries.

According to the details at page 201 of the estimates, there are ninety-five elevator operators. This comes under maintenance and operation of dominion public buildings and grounds. I assume that is in Ottawa?
Yes. According to my notes, there are ninety-six.

Probably the minister has operators for Ottawa and outside Ottawa together. I was particularly concerned about elevator operators in this city. I should like to know how many of them are on the permanent staff. If the minister cannot tell us that, perhaps he can say how many years they have to serve before they become permanent.

They are
appointed by the civil service commission, as are other civil servants, and they have to stay a year on probation, I believe, before they are made permanent. But at the end of the year, if their services have been satisfactory, they are given permanency. I believe they are all returned men who operate our elevators; at least all I know are returned men.
I am not complaining. I just wished to find out how long they must serve before they were placed on the permanent staff.

My understanding is that, according to the Civil Service Act, it is a year. After one year's good service, they are made permanent. However, during the war I believe there was a regulation under which no permanent appointments would be made, until the end of the war, with a view to giving the returned men an equal chance.
How many hours do these men work? Are they on an eight-hour day?
Yes, that is what I have been told. They work on eight-hour shifts, but they do not always work the same shifts.
Would the minister inquire whether or not, after one year of satisfactory service, these elevator men are given permanent appointments? I believe he will find that some are not.
I have not my officials with me, but in my note I see there are two figures. However, the note does show that there are ninety-six permanent and sixty temporary, making a total of 156 in Ottawa.
That is all the more reason the minister should have a careful check made, so as to see that no returned soldier has been on for more than a year without receiving an appointment.

I shall look into that, but I would be most surprised if they did not get permanency. After a year's time, these men know the law quite well as to what they may expect. However, there are still sixty on the temporary staff and ninety-six who are permanent.

The minister may be in for a slight surprise. There is one other matter I would draw to his attention. I realize he cannot know about every detail in his department. I shall look into the matter, although this is the first time I have heard that complaint. I see elevator men during the day in this building, and we are not so strict that we keep them down to a rigid discipline.
I realize that, and I am not complaining; but there may have been some cases the minister did not hear about.

-to service
nearly all our elevators in our buildings. I have received complaints from elevator men to the effect that sometimes they have difficulties with the elevators. speechtext: These elevators get pretty heavy service, for the type they are.

I heard the minister refer to returned soldiers, and I should like to think that after one year's service, if they have given good service they would be permanently employed. I should like to have some assurance to that effect.
My impression is that that is what happens.
I did not get that impression from what was said before.

The Department of Public Works does not appoint elevator men. We send a request to the civil service commission, and they send a man who is on the eligible list. We take him on and, according to the act, at the end of the year if he has rendered good service he becomes a permanent civil servant. If there were any delay, it would not be the department which would be making the permanent appointment; it would be the civil service commission.

In other words, a man may give good service to the minister's department but may not receive the appointment. Any man who has served in the armed forces and who has given good service for a year in the minister's department should receive the appointment.
I agree.
Irrespective of the civil service commission.

I agree, if it is done according to regulations. But in every branch of every department we do not find 100 per cent who are permanent. Some leeway is always allowed; before the war it was ten per cent. I agree that any man who is rendering good service to the government should be made a permanent appointee after a year.

There are a number of revotes here and I should like to ask what check has been made of them. After all, you had the estimates of a year ago and you are revoting money today. How close are the revotes coming to the actual expenditures?

In December,
1945, the department prepared estimates for 1946-47 and those estimates were voted in August, 1946. We prepared plans where the staff was available, but in most cases we did not reach the point where we could even ask for tenders, while in some cases where we asked for tenders we did not receive any bids. If the hon. member will look over the list he will find that in ninety-five per cent of the cases the amounts are the same as we voted last year. They are due to lack of

staff, lack of materials, lack of man-power and the advice received by my department from other departments as to the situation in the country. This year they expect to make more progress on these revotes.

I think the minister is wrong because everybody knows that between last fall and today there has been a distinct increase in prices. I do not see how you can call it a revote when you know that something that was voted last year will cost you more this year. I think the minister should in presenting a revote tell the committee what the increased expenditure will be. If we are revoting an amount I should like to think the job can be done with the money that is being voted today.

Take the first item, for instance, for a customs and immigration building at Armstrong, just to show how it works. This is a revote of $45,000 for the construction of a building for customs and immigration purposes on a government-owned site at Armstrong, Quebec. The proposed building will cost so much. The estimate they give is the same this year as last year. This money has not been spent. We are having plans prepared and we will call for tenders.

The minister says this revote is the same as last year. Anybody in business knows that costs have risen since last year, and I think the minister and his officials are wrong in revoting just the same amount of money they asked for last year.
We do not in every instance.

Take the case of Armstrong which the minister cited. I know that district, and I know that you could not build a custom house in Armstrong today for the same amount you could a year ago. We know there has been an increase in costs, the minister should give some indication of what the increased cost will be. The minister's officials are wrong when they say they could put up a building for 845,000 in Armstrong last year and this year they can do it for the same amount of money.

If my hon. friend will permit me, I will appeal to his own experience. Imagine for a moment that he is minister of public works and that last year in the month of August the amount of 845,000 was submitted to my hon. friend as minister of public works to put up this building. Tenders were asked for in the fall, but it was found impossible to go on with the work because of the

Supply-Public Works
lateness of the season. My hon. friend knows how difficult and how expensive it is to build cement foundations when the weather is very cold. Therefore the building was postponed until this year, and I presume that the department will proceed with the amount of this revote. If the cost is higher this year than last the building will not be completed, and in the estimates next year there will be another item to finish the building. My hon. friend knows that very well.
I will now make a suggestion with which he will probably agree. It is that the estimates of the Department of Public Works should come before us in the early part of the session for several reasons, but especially because it is easier to cut lumber in the winter when the sap is not in the tree, and therefore it may be possible to encourage some people in the vicinity to do the work, which would save a lot of transportation costs. I have enjoyed this discussion very much, which is just as friendly as the one that has been going on with my hon. friend. The tone which has been adopted by the Minister of Public Works makes a great difference. I enjoy discussing things with the hon. member for York South. He is sensible enough to understand that it is impossible to proceed otherwise than as the minister has done, and he is not dogmatic.

I agree with everything the hon. member for Temiscouata has said. I know there are seasonal difficulties which must be overcome, and I am of the opinion that the officers of the department have tried to do a good job for the money that has been placed at their disposal. At the same time, in spite of the seasonal difficulties, it does seem irresponsible from an accounting point of view that the minister should come back to this house and ask for a revote of the same amount of money if he knows it will not do the job. The minister is just as well aware as I am that it will cost more today than it would have cost a year ago. His officials must realize that the money we voted a year ago is not sufficient to do the job they are expected to do today. Yet this amount is put in the estimates as a revote. It is not a revote, because the building will cost us more money, and the minister should tell us how much more it will cost.

In many
instances the items here are the amounts that my officials tell me will be expended during the year. Take the first item for a customs and immigration building at Armstrong. It started off in the fall of 1945 with an estimate of $35,000. When we got
to August we asked for another $10,000 in the supplementary estimates. When the main estimates were prepared in December the item was $45,000, which was the figure of last year's vote. We are in June now. These estimates were prepared in November of last year and they left my office in December to be approved by the government and the treasury board before being printed for the January issue. Estimates in detail like this are prepared in September, October, November and December and then have to be approved. So that the hon. member is reading things which were prepared six months ahead of time.

They are six months
behind. The minister said that last December certain money had been spent. If he will add all that up he will find it is more than the money that was voted a year ago.

We have not
even started to spend this money.
The minister said that at Armstrong there had been spent-
We did not spend a cent.

That is not what the minister said. I may be misinterpreting him and I am willing to admit that; but I think that, having regard to the fact that we are voting certain moneys for certain public projects with which none of us will disagree, unless there is absolute waste, when we voted money a year ago and come back today to revote the same amount it is not sound business practice, and the minister should tell us what the extra cost will be. In his charming way he has tried to tell us that something will happen at Armstrong, but I am positive that what he has said1 does not add up. Two and two are always four, but the minister made some statements that seemed to suggest that two and two made five.

I do not think the hon. gentleman understood what I said. This is an estimate. My architects say that for the site and supervision of that building in Armstrong, we shall need, according to the plans and specifications which we are preparing, $40,000. We will advertise for tenders-
Forty thousand?

The sum of $45,000. We will advertise for tenders and, before I receive them, I shall not know whether they will be below or above this amount of $45,000, nor would the hon. member know.

I am not satisfied to let this thing go right now. We have a tremendous sum of money, millions of dollars being voted>, and I have in my mind as a businessman the necessity for being a little more explicit about these figures. I do not think you can say it is simply a revote from last year, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said.
The hon. gentleman understands what a revote is.

I understand just as well as the minister what a revote is, but it seems to me we are voting money for a specific job and the money is collected from the taxpayers of the country. I know we have to get down and save dollars and cents for the benefit of the people, and it seems to me that if we revote everything, we are not trying to economize on their behalf. I think the Canadian people are perfectly willing to pay a fair shot, but when in public works we disregard everything and come out and vote this and that, which we were prepared to do in war time, and then revote it, the minister should be more explicit. I suggest that he should be more explicit about this revoting. If we are revoting money on the old expenditures it should be increased; it should not be the same amount. If we are revoting it on other grounds, then it should be cancelled completely. I repeat, the minister should be more explicit on the question of revoting. When we read these estimates that are being presented today we see revote after revote. What does it mean? It is the same money we voted last
